lessons.title: States of matter and how they change

story.title: The earthen pot that cools water

scenes.text: In a Rajasthan village, Gauri's grandmother stores drinking water in a clay matka. On a 44 °C day the water stays cool.
Gauri wonders how a pot with no electricity can cool water.
Her science teacher explains: water seeps through tiny pores and evaporates from the outside, taking heat energy with it.
Her pen-pal Lucas in Brazil says people there hang wet cloths in windows for the same reason. Evaporation causes cooling everywhere!

steps.title: What matter is made of
steps.body:
Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. It is made of **tiny particles** that:
- have **spaces** between them (sugar dissolves in water without raising the level much),
- are **continuously moving** (diffusion — the smell of incense spreading through a room),
- **attract** each other (it takes force to break a piece of iron).

Movement increases with temperature: diffusion is faster in hot water than in cold.

steps.title: Three common states
steps.body:
- **Solid**: fixed shape and volume, particles tightly packed, strong attraction, negligible compressibility.
- **Liquid**: fixed volume, takes the shape of the container, flows, slightly compressible.
- **Gas**: no fixed shape or volume, highly compressible (CNG and LPG cylinders), particles far apart and moving fast, exert pressure on walls.

Scientists also describe **plasma** (in stars, neon signs) and **Bose–Einstein condensate** (at extremely low temperatures).

steps.title: Changing state
steps.body:
- **Melting point** of ice: 0 °C (273 K). **Boiling point** of water at normal atmospheric pressure: 100 °C (373 K). K = °C + 273.
- During melting and boiling, temperature **stays constant** even though heat is supplied. That hidden heat is **latent heat** — used to overcome attraction between particles.
- Latent heat of fusion of ice ≈ 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg; latent heat of vaporisation of water ≈ 22.5 × 10⁵ J/kg. That is why steam at 100 °C burns more than boiling water at 100 °C.
- **Sublimation**: solid → gas directly (camphor, naphthalene, dry ice / solid CO₂).

steps.title: Evaporation
steps.body:
Evaporation is a **surface** phenomenon that happens **below** the boiling point. It increases with:
- larger surface area (clothes spread out dry faster),
- higher temperature,
- lower humidity,
- more wind.

**Evaporation causes cooling**: the fastest particles escape, carrying energy away. Examples: clay pots, sweating, acetone feeling cold on skin, wearing cotton in summer (it absorbs sweat and lets it evaporate).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying temperature rises while ice melts. It stays at 0 °C until all ice has melted.
- Confusing evaporation (surface, any temperature) with boiling (whole liquid, fixed temperature).
- Converting K to °C by adding 273 instead of subtracting.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
1. Convert 300 K to °C. (27 °C.)
2. Why do we see water droplets outside a glass of ice water? (Water vapour in air condenses on the cold surface.)
3. Why does a wet cloth dry faster on a windy day? (Wind carries away vapour, increasing evaporation.)

lessons.title: Pure substances, mixtures and separation

scenes.text: Rahim's family runs a dairy in Anand, Gujarat. A customer asks: 'Is your milk pure?'
Rahim's sister, a chemistry student, smiles: 'To a chemist, milk is a mixture — water, fats, proteins, sugars.'
In the dairy, a centrifuge spins milk to separate cream — the same idea used in blood tests at labs.
'Pure' in daily life means unadulterated. In science, a pure substance has only one kind of particle.

steps.title: Pure substances vs mixtures
steps.body:
**Pure substance**: made of one kind of particle with fixed composition and properties.
- **Element**: cannot be broken into simpler substances by chemical means (iron, oxygen, carbon).
- **Compound**: two or more elements chemically combined in a **fixed ratio by mass** (water H₂O — hydrogen and oxygen always 1 : 8 by mass).

**Mixture**: two or more substances mixed in **any proportion**, each keeping its properties.
- **Homogeneous** (uniform): salt solution, air, brass.
- **Heterogeneous** (non-uniform): sand + water, oil + water, iron filings + sulphur.

steps.title: Solutions, suspensions and colloids
steps.body:
- **True solution**: particles < 1 nm, transparent, don't settle, don't scatter light (sugar in water).
- **Colloid**: particles roughly 1–1000 nm, appear uniform, don't settle, **scatter light (Tyndall effect)** — milk, fog, smoke, jelly, shaving cream.
- **Suspension**: large particles, settle on standing, can be filtered (chalk in water, muddy water).

**Concentration** = mass of solute / mass of solution × 100 (mass %). Example: 20 g salt in 180 g water → 20/200 × 100 = **10%**.

steps.title: Separation techniques
steps.body:
- **Evaporation**: salt from salt water.
- **Filtration**: insoluble solid from liquid (sand from water).
- **Centrifugation**: cream from milk, blood cells from plasma.
- **Separating funnel**: immiscible liquids (oil and water).
- **Sublimation**: ammonium chloride or camphor from salt.
- **Chromatography**: colours in ink or dye; detecting drugs in blood.
- **Distillation**: miscible liquids with a large boiling-point difference (acetone and water); **fractional distillation** for close boiling points (separating gases of air, petroleum refining).
- **Crystallisation**: purer crystals of salt or alum (better than evaporation, which leaves soluble impurities).

steps.title: Physical vs chemical change
steps.body:
- **Physical change**: no new substance; often reversible (melting wax, dissolving sugar, tearing paper).
- **Chemical change**: new substance(s) formed with new properties (burning, rusting, cooking, curdling milk).

A burning candle shows both: wax melting is physical; wax burning is chemical.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling air a compound. It is a mixture — its composition varies and each gas keeps its properties.
- Calling brass an element. It is an alloy (a homogeneous mixture of copper and zinc).
- Using evaporation when you want pure crystals — use crystallisation.

lessons.title: Atoms, molecules, formulae and the mole

scenes.text: Shopkeeper Mr. Iyer in Coimbatore never counts rice grains — he weighs them.
Chemist Dr. Amina explains: atoms are far too small to count, so chemists also count by weighing, using a unit called the mole.
One mole of anything contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles — Avogadro's number.
So 18 g of water — about a tablespoonful — holds 6.022 × 10²³ molecules!

steps.title: Laws of chemical combination
steps.body:
- **Law of conservation of mass** (Lavoisier): mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. Total mass of reactants = total mass of products.
- **Law of constant proportions** (Proust): a pure compound always contains the same elements in the same proportion by mass (water: H : O = 1 : 8).

**Dalton's atomic theory** explained these: matter is made of atoms; atoms of an element are identical; atoms combine in small whole-number ratios; atoms are neither created nor destroyed in reactions. (We now know atoms are divisible and isotopes exist.)

steps.title: Symbols, ions and valency
steps.body:
Symbols: H, He, C, N, O, Na (natrium), K (kalium), Fe (ferrum), Cu (cuprum), Ag (argentum), Au (aurum).

**Valency** = combining capacity. Common ions:
- +1: Na⁺, K⁺, Ag⁺, NH₄⁺, H⁺
- +2: Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Zn²⁺, Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺
- +3: Al³⁺, Fe³⁺
- −1: Cl⁻, OH⁻, NO₃⁻, HCO₃⁻
- −2: O²⁻, SO₄²⁻, CO₃²⁻, S²⁻
- −3: PO₄³⁻, N³⁻

**Criss-cross method**: write symbols, exchange valencies as subscripts, simplify. Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ → **Al₂(SO₄)₃**; Ca²⁺ and OH⁻ → **Ca(OH)₂**; Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ → Mg₂O₂ → **MgO**.

steps.title: Atomic mass, molecular mass and the mole
steps.body:
Atomic masses are measured in **u** (unified mass, 1/12 of a carbon-12 atom). H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16, Na = 23, Mg = 24, S = 32, Cl = 35.5, Ca = 40.

**Molecular mass** = sum of atomic masses. H₂O = 2 + 16 = 18 u; CO₂ = 44 u; H₂SO₄ = 2 + 32 + 64 = 98 u. For ionic compounds we say **formula unit mass** (NaCl = 58.5 u).

**1 mole** = 6.022 × 10²³ particles (N₀). **Molar mass** = the same number in grams (water: 18 g/mol).
- moles = given mass / molar mass
- number of particles = moles × 6.022 × 10²³

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1. Moles in 52 g of helium (He = 4): 52/4 = **13 mol**.
2. Mass of 0.5 mol of nitrogen gas N₂: 0.5 × 28 = **14 g**.
3. Number of molecules in 8 g of oxygen gas O₂: 8/32 = 0.25 mol → 0.25 × 6.022 × 10²³ = **1.51 × 10²³ molecules**.
4. Conservation of mass check: 5.3 g sodium carbonate reacts with 6 g ethanoic acid giving 2.2 g CO₂, 0.9 g water and 8.2 g sodium ethanoate. Reactants 11.3 g = products 11.3 g ✔.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing O (atom, 16 u) with O₂ (molecule, 32 u).
- Writing CaOH₂ instead of Ca(OH)₂ — brackets are needed for polyatomic ions taken more than once.
- Writing the subscript as a coefficient: 2H₂O means two molecules; H₂O₂ is a different compound (hydrogen peroxide).

lessons.title: Structure of the atom

scenes.text: In 1909–1911, in Ernest Rutherford's lab, scientists fired tiny alpha particles at a very thin gold foil.
Most went straight through. A few bent. A very few bounced straight back.
Rutherford later said it was almost as incredible as firing a shell at tissue paper and having it come back.
Conclusion: an atom is mostly empty space, with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus. Priyanka, 15, from Shillong, is amazed that so much came from one experiment.

steps.title: Subatomic particles
steps.body:
- **Electron** (e⁻): discovered by J.J. Thomson; charge −1; mass about 1/1836 of a proton.
- **Proton** (p⁺): positive charge +1; mass ≈ 1 u; identified through Goldstein's canal rays and Rutherford's work.
- **Neutron** (n): no charge; mass ≈ 1 u; discovered by James Chadwick in 1932.

Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus; electrons are outside.

steps.title: Three atomic models
steps.body:
- **Thomson (plum pudding / watermelon)**: positive sphere with electrons embedded. Failed to explain Rutherford's results.
- **Rutherford (nuclear model)**: tiny positive nucleus containing almost all the mass; electrons revolve around it; most of the atom is empty. Problem: a revolving charged electron should lose energy and spiral into the nucleus — the atom would be unstable.
- **Bohr**: electrons move in fixed **orbits (shells / energy levels)** K, L, M, N… and do not radiate energy while in them. This explained atomic stability.

steps.title: Electronic configuration (first 20 elements)
steps.body:
Maximum electrons in a shell = **2n²**: K (n = 1) 2, L 8, M 18, N 32. But the **outermost shell holds at most 8**, and shells fill in order (for elements 1–20).

Examples: C (6) 2,4 · O (8) 2,6 · Na (11) 2,8,1 · Cl (17) 2,8,7 · Ar (18) 2,8,8 · K (19) 2,8,8,1 · Ca (20) 2,8,8,2.

**Valency**: if valence electrons are 1–4, valency = that number; if 5–7, valency = 8 − number. Noble gases (full outer shell) have valency 0. Na → 1, Mg → 2, Cl → 1, O → 2, N → 3.

steps.title: Atomic number, mass number, isotopes, isobars
steps.body:
- **Atomic number Z** = number of protons (defines the element).
- **Mass number A** = protons + neutrons. Neutrons = A − Z. Written as ²³₁₁Na (A = 23, Z = 11 → 12 neutrons).
- **Isotopes**: same Z, different A — e.g. ¹²C and ¹⁴C; ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl. Same chemical properties. Chlorine's average atomic mass 35.5 u comes from the mix (about 3 : 1) of ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl.
- Uses: uranium-235 as nuclear fuel; cobalt-60 in cancer treatment; an iodine isotope in treating goitre.
- **Isobars**: same A, different Z — ⁴⁰Ca and ⁴⁰Ar.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing K as 2,8,9 (19 electrons). The outer shell cannot exceed 8 here; correct is 2,8,8,1.
- Confusing mass number with atomic mass (35.5 for Cl is an average, not a mass number).
- Thinking isotopes have different chemical properties — they have the same electrons, so the same chemistry.

lessons.title: Chemical equations and balancing

scenes.text: In her school lab in Dehradun, Simran holds a cleaned magnesium ribbon in a flame with tongs.
It burns with a dazzling white light, leaving white powder.
Her lab partner Ethan, visiting from Kenya, reminds her: 'Don't look straight at the flame — it's very bright.'
The teacher writes: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. 'Every atom you start with must be there at the end.'

steps.title: Signs of a chemical reaction
steps.body:
- change in **state**,
- change in **colour**,
- **evolution of a gas** (bubbles),
- change in **temperature** (heat given out or absorbed),
- formation of a **precipitate**.

Examples: zinc in dilute acid gives bubbles of hydrogen; magnesium burns brightly; lead nitrate and potassium iodide give a yellow precipitate.

steps.title: Word equation to balanced equation
steps.body:
Word: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide.
Skeletal: Mg + O₂ → MgO (unbalanced: 2 O on left, 1 on right).
Balanced: **2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO**.

**Rules:**
- Change only the **coefficients** (numbers in front), never the subscripts.
- Balance the element appearing in the fewest formulae first; leave H and O (or free elements) for last.
- Add state symbols: (s), (l), (g), (aq). Conditions such as heat, light or catalyst go above the arrow.

steps.title: Worked example: Fe + H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + H₂
steps.body:
1. Fe: 1 left, 3 right → 3Fe + H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + H₂
2. O: 1 left, 4 right → 3Fe + 4H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + H₂
3. H: 8 left, 2 right → 3Fe + 4H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂
Check: Fe 3 = 3, H 8 = 8, O 4 = 4 ✔.

**3Fe(s) + 4H₂O(g) → Fe₃O₄(s) + 4H₂(g)**

steps.title: More practice
steps.body:
- CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O (natural gas burning)
- 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂
- 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O
- BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ → BaSO₄↓ + 2NaCl (white precipitate)
- C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O (respiration in our cells)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing H₂O to H₂O₂ to balance oxygen. That changes the substance!
- Forgetting that hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and chlorine gases are diatomic (H₂, O₂, N₂, Cl₂).
- Not re-counting every element at the end.

lessons.title: Types of reactions, redox, corrosion and rancidity

story.title: The rusting bicycle and the stale chips

scenes.text: Vivek leaves his bicycle outside during the Mumbai monsoon. In weeks, orange-brown rust appears.
Meanwhile an open packet of chips in the kitchen tastes and smells bad.
His aunt, a food scientist, says: 'Both are oxidation — oxygen reacting slowly.'
'That's why chip packets are filled with nitrogen and bicycles are painted.'

steps.title: Combination and decomposition
steps.body:
**Combination**: two or more substances form one product.
- CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq) + heat (slaked lime for whitewashing)
- C + O₂ → CO₂

**Decomposition**: one substance breaks into simpler ones.
- **Thermal**: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (heat); 2FeSO₄ → Fe₂O₃ + SO₂ + SO₃ (green crystals turn brown on heating)
- **Electrolytic**: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ (electricity; hydrogen volume is twice the oxygen volume)
- **Photolytic**: 2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂ (sunlight; used in black-and-white photography)

**Exothermic** reactions release heat (burning, respiration); **endothermic** reactions absorb heat (most decompositions).

steps.title: Displacement and double displacement
steps.body:
**Displacement**: a more reactive element displaces a less reactive one.
- Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu (blue solution turns pale green; iron nail gets a brown copper coat)
- Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu

**Double displacement**: exchange of ions between two compounds.
- Na₂SO₄ + BaCl₂ → BaSO₄↓ (white) + 2NaCl
- Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2KI → PbI₂↓ (yellow) + 2KNO₃
A reaction that forms an insoluble solid is a **precipitation reaction**. Acid + base → salt + water (neutralisation) is also double displacement.

steps.title: Oxidation and reduction (redox)
steps.body:
- **Oxidation**: gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen.
- **Reduction**: loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen.
Both happen together — **redox**.

CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O: CuO is **reduced** (loses O); H₂ is **oxidised** (gains O). H₂ is the **reducing agent**, CuO the **oxidising agent**.

ZnO + C → Zn + CO: ZnO reduced, C oxidised.

steps.title: Corrosion and rancidity
steps.body:
**Corrosion**: metals are attacked by moisture, air, acids — **rusting of iron** (needs both air and water), black coating on silver (silver sulphide), green coating on copper (basic copper carbonate). Corrosion damages bridges, ships and cars; prevention: painting, oiling, greasing, galvanising (zinc coating), alloying.

**Rancidity**: oxidation of fats and oils in food, changing smell and taste. Prevention: airtight containers, refrigeration, adding antioxidants, flushing packets with **nitrogen**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the oxidising agent is the substance that gets oxidised. The oxidising agent gets **reduced** (it gives oxygen away).
- Calling every reaction with two reactants 'combination'. Check: is there only one product?
- Thinking rusting needs only water — it needs oxygen too.

lessons.title: Acids and bases

story.title: The bee sting at the picnic

scenes.text: At a picnic in Nainital, a bee stings 9-year-old Rohit. He cries in pain.
His cousin Anjali, who loves chemistry, asks for baking soda from the picnic basket.
After gently removing the sting, she dabs a paste of baking soda and water on the spot. The pain eases.
'The sting injects an acid; baking soda is mildly basic — it neutralises some of it,' she explains. (For allergic reactions, get medical help immediately.)

steps.title: Acids and bases around you
steps.body:
**Acids** taste sour, turn blue litmus red, and produce **H⁺ (H₃O⁺) ions** in water. Natural acids: citric (lemons, oranges), lactic (curd), tartaric (tamarind), acetic/ethanoic (vinegar), oxalic (tomato), methanoic (ant and nettle stings).
**Bases** taste bitter, feel soapy, turn red litmus blue, and produce **OH⁻ ions** in water. Bases soluble in water are **alkalis** (NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)₂).

**Never taste or touch laboratory chemicals** — use indicators.

steps.title: Indicators
steps.body:
- **Litmus** (from lichen): red in acid, blue in base.
- **Phenolphthalein**: colourless in acid, **pink** in base.
- **Methyl orange**: red in acid, yellow in base.
- **Turmeric**: yellow, turns **reddish-brown** with bases.
- **Olfactory indicators**: onion and vanilla lose their smell in basic solutions.
- Red cabbage juice and hibiscus petals also change colour.

steps.title: Reactions of acids
steps.body:
- **Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen**: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂↑ (gas burns with a 'pop').
- **Acid + metal carbonate/hydrogencarbonate → salt + water + CO₂**: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂ (CO₂ turns lime water milky).
- **Acid + base → salt + water** (neutralisation): NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O.
- **Acid + metal oxide → salt + water**: CuO + 2HCl → CuCl₂ + H₂O (blue-green solution). Metal oxides are basic.

Non-metal oxides (CO₂, SO₂) are acidic: Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O.

steps.title: Safety: diluting acids
steps.body:
**Always add acid to water slowly, with stirring — never water to acid.** Diluting concentrated acid is highly exothermic; adding water to acid can make it boil and splash, causing burns and breaking glass.

Wear goggles and gloves in the lab. If acid spills on skin, wash with plenty of running water and tell the teacher immediately.

steps.title: Strength and conductivity
steps.body:
Acids conduct electricity in water because they form ions; dry HCl gas or glucose solution does not change litmus or conduct, because no ions form.

**Strong acids** (HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃) ionise almost completely; **weak acids** (acetic, citric) only partly. *Strong* is not the same as *concentrated*: concentration is how much acid is in the water.

lessons.title: pH and salts in daily life

scenes.text: Lalitha farms in Kerala. Her crops grow poorly, and the agriculture officer tests the soil: pH 5.
'Your soil is too acidic,' says the officer. 'Add agricultural lime or another base the department recommends.'
That evening her son brushes his teeth. The toothpaste is basic too — it fights mouth acids that cause tooth decay.
From soil to stomach to teeth, the pH number matters everywhere.

steps.title: The pH scale
steps.body:
pH (from German *potenz*, power) runs from about **0 to 14**:
- **pH < 7 → acidic** (lower = more acidic)
- **pH = 7 → neutral** (pure water)
- **pH > 7 → basic** (higher = more basic)

Each step of 1 is a **10-fold** change in H⁺ concentration. **Universal indicator** shows different colours across the pH range.

steps.title: pH in everyday life
steps.body:
- **Our body** works within a narrow pH range (blood is slightly basic, about 7.4).
- **Stomach** makes hydrochloric acid to help digestion; excess causes acidity — **antacids** like milk of magnesia (Mg(OH)₂) neutralise it.
- **Tooth decay** starts when mouth pH falls below about 5.5 as bacteria break down sugars; tooth enamel (calcium hydroxyapatite) gets attacked. Brush after meals; toothpaste is basic.
- **Soil**: most crops prefer a near-neutral pH; acidic soil is treated with lime.
- **Acid rain** (rain pH below 5.6) harms lakes and buildings.
- **Stings**: bee stings and nettle stings (methanoic acid) — mild bases like baking soda can soothe.

steps.title: Salts and their families
steps.body:
A salt forms from an acid and a base. Salt families share ions: NaCl and Na₂SO₄ (sodium salts); NaCl and KCl (chloride salts).

pH of salt solutions:
- strong acid + strong base → **neutral** (NaCl)
- strong acid + weak base → **acidic** (NH₄Cl)
- weak acid + strong base → **basic** (CH₃COONa, NaHCO₃)

**Chlor-alkali process**: electrolysis of brine 2NaCl(aq) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + Cl₂(g) + H₂(g). Products used for soaps, PVC, bleach, fuels.

steps.title: Five important salts
steps.body:
- **Bleaching powder** (CaOCl₂): Ca(OH)₂ + Cl₂ → CaOCl₂ + H₂O. Bleaching cotton, disinfecting drinking water.
- **Baking soda** (NaHCO₃): on heating 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂. Baking powder = baking soda + a mild edible acid (like tartaric acid) — the CO₂ makes cakes rise. Also used in antacids and soda-acid fire extinguishers.
- **Washing soda** (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O): removes permanent hardness of water, cleaning, glass making.
- **Plaster of Paris** (CaSO₄·½H₂O): made by heating gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) at 373 K; mixes with water to set hard back into gypsum. Used for fracture casts, statues, smooth walls. Store it dry.
- **Water of crystallisation**: blue copper sulphate crystals (CuSO₄·5H₂O) turn white on heating as they lose water; adding water turns them blue again.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking pH 2 is only 'a little' more acidic than pH 3. It has 10 times more H⁺.
- Calling baking soda 'washing soda'. Baking soda is NaHCO₃; washing soda is Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.
- Writing bleaching powder as CaCl₂ — it is represented as CaOCl₂.

bands.text: Strongly acidic: like the acid in your stomach or a car battery. Corrosive.
Acidic: lemon juice and vinegar (about 2–3), tomato and orange juice (about 4).
Weakly acidic: black coffee, normal rain (≈ 5.6), many soils. Tooth enamel is attacked below about 5.5.
Weakly basic: blood (≈ 7.4), sea water, baking soda solution.
Basic: milk of magnesia (≈ 10), toothpaste and soap solutions.

lessons.title: Metals and non-metals: properties and reactivity

scenes.text: In Thrissur's jewellery market, goldsmith Mr. Varghese beats a tiny ball of gold into an incredibly thin sheet.
His granddaughter Ann asks why gold never rusts while the iron gate outside does.
He shows her a chart called the reactivity series: gold sits at the very bottom — it hardly reacts with anything.
Sodium sits near the top — so reactive it's stored under kerosene.

steps.title: Physical properties
steps.body:
**Metals**: lustrous, hard (except sodium and potassium, which can be cut with a knife), **malleable** (gold and silver are the most malleable), **ductile** (drawn into wires), good **conductors** of heat and electricity (silver and copper the best), **sonorous** (school bells), high melting points (except **gallium and caesium**, which melt near body temperature in the palm), solid at room temperature (except **mercury**, a liquid).

**Non-metals**: usually dull, brittle, poor conductors; solids, liquid (**bromine**) or gases. Exceptions: **iodine** is lustrous; **graphite** conducts electricity; **diamond** (carbon) is the hardest natural substance.

steps.title: Chemical properties of metals
steps.body:
- **With oxygen** → metal oxides (basic): 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO (black). Al₂O₃ and ZnO are **amphoteric** — they react with both acids and bases.
- **With water**: sodium and potassium react violently with cold water (stored in kerosene); calcium reacts less violently (floats due to H₂ bubbles); magnesium reacts with hot water; Al, Fe, Zn react with steam; Pb, Cu, Ag, Au don't react with water.
- **With dilute acids** → salt + hydrogen (not with Cu, Ag, Au). With nitric acid, H₂ is usually not obtained because HNO₃ is a strong oxidising agent (except with Mg and Mn with very dilute HNO₃).
- **Displacement**: more reactive metals displace less reactive ones from their salt solutions.

steps.title: Reactivity series
steps.body:
From most to least reactive:
**K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au**

Memory aid: '**K**ing **Na**sir **Ca**n **M**ake **A**ll **Z**ebras **F**eel **P**retty **H**appy, **C**ute **H**ens **S**ing **G**lee.'

Metals above hydrogen displace it from dilute acids; those below cannot.

steps.title: Ionic compounds
steps.body:
Metals lose electrons, non-metals gain them: Na (2,8,1) → Na⁺ (2,8) + e⁻; Cl (2,8,7) + e⁻ → Cl⁻ (2,8,8). The ions attract strongly to form **NaCl**.

Properties of ionic compounds: hard, brittle solids; **high melting and boiling points**; soluble in water, insoluble in kerosene/petrol; **conduct electricity when molten or in solution** (ions free to move) but not as solids.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all metals are solids (mercury is liquid) or all non-metals don't conduct (graphite conducts).
- Thinking copper reacts with dilute HCl. It is below hydrogen.
- Saying solid NaCl conducts — only molten or dissolved.

lessons.title: Extraction of metals and corrosion

scenes.text: On a field trip to a steel plant in Jamshedpur, Aryan sees reddish-brown iron ore entering a huge blast furnace.
The engineer, Ms. Kaur, explains that carbon (from coke) takes oxygen away from the ore.
Later, she shows a video of railway workers joining tracks using the 'thermit' reaction, where aluminium grabs oxygen from iron oxide so fiercely that molten iron forms.
And the famous Iron Pillar in Delhi has resisted rusting for over 1,600 years!

steps.title: Minerals and ores
steps.body:
Metals occur in the Earth's crust as **minerals**; minerals from which a metal can be profitably extracted are **ores**. Unwanted impurities like sand and soil are **gangue**.

The extraction method depends on reactivity:
- **Low reactivity** (Hg, Cu): heating the ore alone. HgS roasted → HgO → Hg.
- **Middle** (Zn, Fe, Pb): roasting/calcination to oxide, then **reduction with carbon**.
- **High** (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al): **electrolysis** of molten compounds (they are too reactive for carbon).

steps.title: Roasting, calcination, reduction
steps.body:
- **Roasting**: heating **sulphide** ores strongly in excess air: 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂.
- **Calcination**: heating **carbonate** ores in limited air: ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂.
- **Reduction**: ZnO + C → Zn + CO.
- **Thermit reaction**: Fe₂O₃ + 2Al → 2Fe + Al₂O₃ + lots of heat — molten iron welds rail tracks and cracked machine parts.

steps.title: Electrolytic refining
steps.body: Impure copper is made the **anode**, a thin strip of pure copper the **cathode**, and acidified copper sulphate the electrolyte. On passing current, copper dissolves from the anode and deposits as pure copper on the cathode; impurities collect below the anode as **anode mud**. Zinc, silver, gold and others are also refined electrolytically.

steps.title: Preventing corrosion
steps.body:
- Painting, oiling, greasing
- **Galvanising**: coating iron or steel with zinc (even if scratched, zinc corrodes first and protects the iron)
- Chrome plating, anodising aluminium
- **Alloying**: stainless steel (iron with chromium and nickel) does not rust easily. Other alloys: brass (Cu + Zn), bronze (Cu + Sn), solder (Pb + Sn, low melting point). 22-carat gold is 22 parts gold to 2 parts copper or silver, harder than pure 24-carat gold.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing roasting (sulphides, excess air) and calcination (carbonates, limited air).
- Thinking sodium can be obtained by heating its oxide with carbon — it is too reactive.
- In refining, the impure metal is the **anode**, not the cathode.

lessons.title: Carbon: bonding, hydrocarbons and naming

scenes.text: Over breakfast in Hyderabad, Sana's father lists things containing carbon: bread, milk, her cotton shirt, the LPG in the stove, her own body.
'And the pencil lead,' adds her brother. 'Graphite — pure carbon.'
'And Mum's diamond earrings,' laughs Sana. 'Also pure carbon!'
Carbon's special talent is linking with itself into chains and rings — millions of compounds.

steps.title: Covalent bonding
steps.body:
Carbon (2,4) has 4 valence electrons. Gaining or losing 4 would need too much energy, so it **shares** electrons — **covalent bonds**.
- H₂: single bond H–H
- O₂: double bond O=O
- N₂: triple bond N≡N
- CH₄ (methane): carbon shares one pair with each of 4 hydrogens.

Covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points and do not conduct electricity (no ions).

steps.title: Why so many carbon compounds?
steps.body:
- **Catenation**: carbon forms long chains, branches and rings with itself.
- **Tetravalency**: it bonds to 4 other atoms (C, H, O, N, S, Cl…).

**Allotropes of carbon**: diamond (each C bonded to 4 others in a rigid 3D network — hardest natural substance, does not conduct), graphite (layers of hexagons; each C bonded to 3 others — soft, slippery, conducts electricity), and **fullerenes** such as C₆₀ (football-shaped).

steps.title: Hydrocarbons and homologous series
steps.body:
- **Alkanes** (saturated, single bonds): CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ — methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈, butane C₄H₁₀.
- **Alkenes** (one C=C): CₙH₂ₙ — ethene C₂H₄, propene C₃H₆.
- **Alkynes** (one C≡C): CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ — ethyne C₂H₂.

A **homologous series** has the same functional group and general formula; successive members differ by **–CH₂–** (14 u). Chemical properties are similar; physical properties (boiling point) change gradually. Butane has **isomers**: n-butane (straight) and isobutane (branched) — same formula, different structure.

steps.title: Functional groups and naming
steps.body:
Prefix/word root by carbon count: **meth** (1), **eth** (2), **prop** (3), **but** (4), **pent** (5), **hex** (6).
- Halo (–Cl, –Br): prefix chloro-/bromo- → chloropropane
- Alcohol (–OH): suffix **-ol** → ethanol C₂H₅OH
- Aldehyde (–CHO): **-al** → methanal HCHO
- Ketone (C=O inside chain): **-one** → propanone CH₃COCH₃
- Carboxylic acid (–COOH): **-oic acid** → ethanoic acid CH₃COOH
- Double bond: **-ene**, triple: **-yne**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking graphite doesn't conduct because it's a non-metal. It conducts due to free electrons between layers.
- Writing ethene as C₂H₆. Ethene (alkene) is C₂H₄; ethane is C₂H₆.
- Forgetting that propanone needs at least 3 carbons (a ketone cannot have 1 or 2).

story.title: How soap rescues a greasy plate

scenes.text: After a big biryani dinner in Lucknow, Zoya scrubs an oily plate with plain water. The grease won't budge.
Adding soap, the oil lifts away in seconds.
Her chemistry teacher, Mr. Thomas, later explains that soap molecules have a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail.
The tails grab the oil, forming tiny balls called micelles that water rinses away.

steps.title: Four important reaction types
steps.body:
1. **Combustion**: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + heat and light. Saturated hydrocarbons burn with a clean blue flame; unsaturated ones give a yellow sooty flame. (A blackened cooking-vessel bottom means the air holes of the stove are blocked — fuel is burning incompletely.)
2. **Oxidation**: ethanol → ethanoic acid using **alkaline KMnO₄** or **acidified K₂Cr₂O₇** (oxidising agents).
3. **Addition (hydrogenation)**: unsaturated vegetable oils + H₂ in the presence of **nickel or palladium catalyst** → saturated fats (vanaspati). Animal fats and hydrogenated fats are high in saturated fats; oils with unsaturated fatty acids are considered healthier.
4. **Substitution**: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl (in sunlight).

steps.title: Ethanol (C₂H₅OH)
steps.body:
- Liquid at room temperature, soluble in water; the active ingredient of alcoholic drinks, also used in medicines (tinctures), as a solvent and as fuel (blended with petrol).
- 2Na + 2C₂H₅OH → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂ (sodium ethoxide; hydrogen evolved).
- With hot concentrated H₂SO₄ at 443 K: C₂H₅OH → C₂H₄ + H₂O (dehydration).
- **Health note**: drinking alcohol harms health, especially for young people; consuming methanol, even in small amounts, can cause blindness and death. Industrial ethanol is 'denatured' with poisons and dyes to prevent misuse.

steps.title: Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH)
steps.body:
- **Vinegar** is about 5–8% ethanoic acid in water. Pure ethanoic acid freezes at about 290 K (17 °C) in cold weather — hence 'glacial acetic acid'.
- Weak acid; reacts with bases and with carbonates: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂.
- **Esterification**: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O (with conc. H₂SO₄ catalyst). Esters smell sweet/fruity — used in perfumes and flavours.
- **Saponification**: ester + NaOH → alcohol + sodium salt of the acid; this reaction is used to make soap.

steps.title: Soaps and detergents
steps.body:
**Soaps** are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids. Each molecule has an **ionic (hydrophilic) head** and a long **hydrocarbon (hydrophobic) tail**. In water they form **micelles** with tails pointing inward, trapping oil and grease in the centre; rinsing carries them away.

**Hard water** contains calcium and magnesium salts; soap reacts with them to form insoluble **scum**, wasting soap. **Detergents** (sodium salts of sulphonic acids or ammonium salts) do not form scum, so they work in hard water. Some detergents are less biodegradable and can pollute water bodies.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying hydrogenation needs no catalyst — Ni or Pd is required.
- Confusing esterification (acid + alcohol → ester) with saponification (ester + base → soap + alcohol).
- Thinking soap's head is attracted to oil. The **tail** is.

lessons.title: Periodic classification of elements

scenes.text: In 1869, Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev wrote the properties of each known element on cards and arranged them like a game of patience.
He boldly left gaps, predicting elements no one had found — one he called eka-aluminium.
In 1875, gallium was discovered, matching his predictions closely.
Today Aditi in Pune and Kwame in Accra study the same modern periodic table — a map of all matter.

steps.title: Early attempts
steps.body:
- **Döbereiner's triads** (1817 onwards): groups of three similar elements where the middle element's atomic mass is about the average of the other two — Li (7), Na (23), K (39); Ca, Sr, Ba; Cl, Br, I. Only a few triads could be found.
- **Newlands' law of octaves** (1866): arranged by increasing atomic mass, every eighth element had similar properties, like notes in music. Worked only up to calcium.

steps.title: Mendeleev's periodic law
steps.body:
**Properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses.** Mendeleev arranged the 63 known elements, using formulas of oxides and hydrides.

**Achievements**: left gaps and predicted eka-boron (scandium), eka-aluminium (gallium) and eka-silicon (germanium); noble gases discovered later fitted in as a new group.
**Limitations**: no fixed position for hydrogen; isotopes (different masses, same element) had no place; in places a heavier element had to come before a lighter one (cobalt 58.9 before nickel 58.7).

steps.title: The modern periodic table
steps.body:
In 1913, Henry Moseley showed that **atomic number** is the more fundamental property.
**Modern periodic law: properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.**
- **18 groups** (vertical columns): same number of valence electrons → similar properties.
- **7 periods** (horizontal rows): same number of shells. Period 1 has 2 elements, periods 2 and 3 have 8 each.
- Metals on the left, non-metals on the right (top right), **metalloids** (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) along the zig-zag border.

steps.title: Trends
steps.body:
**Across a period (left → right):**
- atomic radius **decreases** (more nuclear charge pulls electrons closer)
- metallic character **decreases**, non-metallic character increases
- valency rises 1 → 4, then falls to 0 (Na 1, Mg 2, Al 3, Si 4, P 3, S 2, Cl 1, Ar 0)
- oxides change from basic to acidic

**Down a group:**
- atomic radius **increases** (new shells)
- metallic character **increases** (easier to lose electrons) — e.g. K is more reactive than Na
- valency stays the same

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying atomic size increases across a period. It decreases.
- Confusing groups (vertical) with periods (horizontal).
- Saying Mendeleev used atomic number — he used atomic mass; Moseley introduced atomic number as the basis.

lessons.title: Rational and irrational numbers

scenes.text: Ananya in Pune is tiling a square courtyard of area 2 m². Her uncle asks: how long is each side?
Her calculator says 1.41421356… and the digits keep going without any repeating pattern.
Her friend Leo in Nairobi says: 'Just write it as a fraction.' Ananya tries 7/5, 141/100, 1414/1000 — none of them squares to exactly 2.
Her teacher smiles: 'You have met an irrational number. Mathematicians proved over 2,000 years ago that no fraction can ever equal √2.'

steps.title: The family of real numbers
steps.body:
- **Natural numbers** N: 1, 2, 3, …
- **Whole numbers** W: 0, 1, 2, 3, …
- **Integers** Z: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …
- **Rational numbers** Q: any number that can be written as p/q where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0 (e.g. 3, −4/7, 0.25, 0.333…).
- **Irrational numbers**: real numbers that *cannot* be written as p/q, e.g. √2, √3, √5, π.

Rational and irrational numbers together make the **real numbers** R. Every real number is a unique point on the number line, and every point on the number line is a real number.

steps.title: Decimal expansions tell you the type
steps.body:
- A rational number has a decimal expansion that either **terminates** (3/8 = 0.375) or is **non-terminating recurring** (1/7 = 0.142857142857…).
- An irrational number has a **non-terminating, non-recurring** expansion (√2 = 1.41421356…).

**Shortcut for fractions in lowest terms p/q:** the decimal terminates exactly when the prime factors of q are only 2s and/or 5s. So 7/40 terminates (40 = 2³ × 5) but 7/30 does not (30 has a factor 3).

steps.title: Worked example: turning 0.4747… into p/q
steps.body:
Let x = 0.474747…
The repeating block has 2 digits, so multiply by 100:
100x = 47.474747…
Subtract: 100x − x = 47.4747… − 0.4747…
99x = 47, so **x = 47/99**.

For 1.2333… (only the 3 repeats): let x = 1.2333…, then 10x = 12.333… and 100x = 123.333…. Subtract: 90x = 111, x = 111/90 = **37/30**.

steps.title: Proof that √2 is irrational (board favourite)
steps.body:
**Proof by contradiction.** Suppose √2 is rational. Then √2 = a/b where a, b are integers with no common factor (lowest terms), b ≠ 0.

Squaring: 2 = a²/b², so a² = 2b². Hence a² is even, so **a is even** (if a prime divides a², it divides a). Write a = 2c.

Then 4c² = 2b², so b² = 2c². Hence b² is even, so **b is even**.

Now a and b are both even — they share the factor 2. This contradicts 'no common factor'. So our assumption is false and **√2 is irrational**. The same method proves √3, √5 and any √p (p prime) are irrational.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying π = 22/7. 22/7 is only an *approximation*; π is irrational.
- Thinking √4 is irrational. √4 = 2, which is rational. Only square roots of non-perfect squares (of positive integers) are irrational.
- Thinking 'irrational + irrational is always irrational'. Counter-example: (2 + √3) + (2 − √3) = 4.
- Forgetting that the sum or product of a non-zero rational and an irrational is always irrational: 3 + √2, 5√2 are irrational.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
1. Without dividing, decide whether 13/125 and 11/12 terminate.
2. Write 0.666… as p/q.
3. Prove that 3 + 2√5 is irrational (hint: assume it equals a rational r, then √5 = (r − 3)/2 would be rational — contradiction).

*Answers:* 1) 125 = 5³ terminates; 12 = 2² × 3 does not. 2) 2/3.

lessons.title: Prime factorisation, HCF and LCM

scenes.text: Kabir in Chennai notices two buses leave the depot together at 8:00 am. Route A returns every 18 minutes, Route B every 24 minutes.
He wonders: when will they next leave together?
Meanwhile his sister Sana has 36 toffees and 48 chocolates to pack into identical gift bags with nothing left over. What is the largest number of bags?
Both puzzles are solved by the same tool: breaking numbers into primes.

steps.title: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
steps.body:
**Every composite number can be written as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique apart from the order of the factors.**

Example: 360 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 = 2³ × 3² × 5. No other set of primes multiplies to 360.

Use a factor tree or repeated division by the smallest prime: 360 → 180 → 90 → 45 → 15 → 5 → 1 (dividing by 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 5).

steps.title: HCF and LCM from primes
steps.body:
Write both numbers in prime-power form.
- **HCF** = product of the *common* primes, each with the **smallest** power.
- **LCM** = product of *all* primes that appear, each with the **largest** power.

For two numbers a and b: **HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b**. (This does NOT hold in general for three numbers.)

steps.title: Worked example: the buses and the gift bags
steps.body:
18 = 2 × 3², 24 = 2³ × 3.
LCM = 2³ × 3² = 72. So the buses leave together again after **72 minutes**, at **9:12 am**.

36 = 2² × 3², 48 = 2⁴ × 3.
HCF = 2² × 3 = 12. Sana can make **12 bags**, each with 3 toffees and 4 chocolates.

Check for 18, 24: HCF = 6, LCM = 72, and 6 × 72 = 432 = 18 × 24 ✔.

steps.title: Which one do I need — HCF or LCM?
steps.body:
- 'Largest size that divides / fits exactly', 'maximum number of groups', 'longest tape that measures exactly' → **HCF**.
- 'Next time together', 'smallest number divisible by all', 'least length that can be measured by all' → **LCM**.

If the answer must be *bigger* than the given numbers, it is an LCM; if *smaller*, an HCF.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the largest powers for HCF (that is LCM).
- Applying HCF × LCM = product to three numbers.
- Claiming a number like 6ⁿ can end in 0: it cannot, because ending in 0 needs prime factor 5, and 6ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 3ⁿ has no 5 (uniqueness of factorisation).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
1. Find HCF and LCM of 96 and 404. (96 = 2⁵ × 3, 404 = 2² × 101 → HCF 4, LCM 9696.)
2. HCF of two numbers is 9 and their LCM is 360. One number is 45. Find the other. (9 × 360 ÷ 45 = 72.)
3. Explain why 7 × 11 × 13 + 13 is composite. (= 13 × (77 + 1) = 13 × 78.)

quiz.why: A number ending in 0 is divisible by 10 = 2 × 5. By uniqueness of prime factorisation, 4ⁿ has only the prime 2.

quiz.q: Two ropes of 64 m and 80 m must be cut into equal pieces of the greatest possible length. Each piece is:
quiz.why: Greatest length that divides both = HCF(64, 80) = 16 m.

lessons.title: Polynomials and their zeros

scenes.text: Meera, a 15-year-old fast bowler in Indore, films her throws. Her coach fits the path of the ball with the expression h(x) = −x² + 6x.
She wants to know where the ball is at ground level, i.e. where h(x) = 0.
Factorising gives −x(x − 6) = 0, so x = 0 (where she releases) and x = 6 (where it lands).
Those two values are the **zeros** of the polynomial — and they are where the graph cuts the x-axis.

steps.title: What is a polynomial?
steps.body:
A polynomial in x is an expression like aₙxⁿ + … + a₁x + a₀ where the powers of x are **whole numbers** (0, 1, 2, …) and the coefficients are real numbers.
- Degree 1: **linear** (2x + 3)
- Degree 2: **quadratic** (x² − 5x + 6)
- Degree 3: **cubic** (x³ − 2x)

NOT polynomials: 1/x (power −1), √x (power 1/2), x + 2/x².

The **degree** is the highest power with a non-zero coefficient. A non-zero constant like 7 has degree 0; the zero polynomial's degree is not defined.

steps.title: Zeros and graphs
steps.body:
A **zero** of p(x) is a number k with p(k) = 0.
- A linear polynomial ax + b has exactly one zero: −b/a. Its graph is a straight line crossing the x-axis once.
- A quadratic has **at most 2** zeros; its graph is a parabola (opening up if a > 0, down if a < 0) that may cut the x-axis at 2 points, touch it at 1, or miss it.
- A cubic has at most 3 zeros.

Geometrically, **the zeros are the x-coordinates where the graph meets the x-axis.**

steps.title: Zeros and coefficients
steps.body:
For quadratic ax² + bx + c with zeros α and β:
- **α + β = −b/a**
- **αβ = c/a**

For cubic ax³ + bx² + cx + d with zeros α, β, γ:
- α + β + γ = −b/a
- αβ + βγ + γα = c/a
- αβγ = −d/a

A quadratic with given sum S and product P of zeros is **k(x² − Sx + P)** for any non-zero constant k.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Find the zeros of x² − 2x − 8 and verify the relationships.

Split the middle term: we need two numbers with product −8 and sum −2: −4 and 2.
x² − 4x + 2x − 8 = x(x − 4) + 2(x − 4) = (x − 4)(x + 2).
Zeros: **4 and −2**.

Check: sum = 2 = −(−2)/1 ✔; product = −8 = −8/1 ✔.

**Reverse problem:** find a quadratic whose zeros have sum −3 and product 2: x² + 3x + 2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sign error: the sum of zeros is **−b/a**, not b/a.
- Writing the zeros of (x − 4)(x + 2) as −4 and 2. Set each factor to 0: x = 4, x = −2.
- Thinking every quadratic has two real zeros. x² + 1 has none: its graph never meets the x-axis.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body:
1. Find the zeros of 6x² − 3 − 7x. (Rewrite 6x² − 7x − 3 = (3x + 1)(2x − 3); zeros −1/3, 3/2.)
2. If α and β are zeros of x² − 5x + 6, find α² + β². (α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ = 25 − 12 = 13.)
3. Write a quadratic with zeros √2 and −√2. (x² − 2.)

lessons.title: Remainder theorem, factor theorem and factorising cubics

story.title: Arjun's shortcut in the exam hall

scenes.text: Arjun in Lucknow faces a question: find the remainder when x³ + 3x² + 3x + 1 is divided by x + 1.
Long division would take five minutes. His friend Zoe in Singapore once told him about a shortcut.
He simply substitutes x = −1: (−1)³ + 3(1) + 3(−1) + 1 = 0. The remainder is 0 — so x + 1 is a factor!
Thirty seconds, full marks. Let's learn exactly why this works.

steps.title: Division algorithm for polynomials
steps.body:
For polynomials p(x) and g(x) ≠ 0 there are unique q(x) and r(x) with
**p(x) = g(x) × q(x) + r(x)**, where r(x) = 0 or degree r < degree g.

Just like 17 = 5 × 3 + 2 for numbers. When dividing by a linear divisor, the remainder is a constant.

steps.title: Remainder and factor theorems
steps.body:
**Remainder theorem:** when p(x) is divided by (x − a), the remainder is **p(a)**.
Why: p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + r; put x = a to get p(a) = r.

For divisor (ax − b), the remainder is p(b/a). For (x + a), use p(−a).

**Factor theorem:** (x − a) is a factor of p(x) **if and only if p(a) = 0**.

steps.title: Worked example: factorise x³ − 23x² + 142x − 120
steps.body:
Try divisors of the constant term 120: p(1) = 1 − 23 + 142 − 120 = 0. So **(x − 1) is a factor**.

Divide: x³ − 23x² + 142x − 120 = (x − 1)(x² − 22x + 120).
Factorise the quadratic: numbers with product 120 and sum −22 are −10 and −12.

So p(x) = **(x − 1)(x − 10)(x − 12)**.

Check: product of zeros 1 × 10 × 12 = 120 = −d/a = −(−120)/1 ✔.

steps.title: Worked example: finding an unknown coefficient
steps.body:
If x³ + ax² − 2x + a + 4 has (x + a) as a factor, find a.

By factor theorem p(−a) = 0:
−a³ + a·a² + 2a + a + 4 = 0 → −a³ + a³ + 3a + 4 = 0 → 3a = −4 → **a = −4/3**.

steps.title: Useful identities
steps.body:
- (a + b)³ = a³ + b³ + 3ab(a + b)
- (a − b)³ = a³ − b³ − 3ab(a − b)
- a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²)
- a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²)
- a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca)

So if a + b + c = 0, then **a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc**. Example: (−12)³ + 7³ + 5³ = 3(−12)(7)(5) = −1260.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Substituting x = +1 for the divisor (x + 1). Use the value that makes the divisor zero: x = −1.
- Forgetting to include a missing term as 0 in long division (write x³ + 0x² − 2x + 1).
- Stopping after finding one factor; factorise the remaining quadratic too.

lessons.title: France before 1789: a society of estates

scenes.text: Imagine Jacques, a peasant near Paris in 1788. A bad harvest has doubled the price of bread.
He must pay the taille (a direct tax) to the state, a tithe to the Church, and dues to the local lord — while nobles and clergy are largely exempt.
In a café in town, his cousin Marie hears people reading aloud from Rousseau and Montesquieu about rights and the people's will.
'Why should birth decide who pays and who rules?' she asks. Many in France were asking the same.

steps.title: The three estates
steps.body:
French society (the 'Old Regime') was divided into **estates**:
- **First Estate**: clergy.
- **Second Estate**: nobility.
- **Third Estate**: everyone else — big businessmen, merchants, lawyers, peasants, artisans, servants. About **90% of people were peasants**, but only a small share of them owned land.

The first two estates enjoyed **privileges by birth**, including exemption from most taxes paid to the state. The Third Estate carried the tax burden: the **taille** (direct tax) and indirect taxes on salt and tobacco, plus the Church's **tithe** (one-tenth of agricultural produce).

steps.title: Economic crisis
steps.body:
- **Louis XVI** became king in **1774** and found the treasury empty after long wars, including the cost of helping the American colonies win independence from Britain.
- Debt grew; lenders charged 10% interest; the state raised taxes.
- France's population grew from about 23 million (1715) to 28 million (1789). Food demand rose faster than grain production; **bread prices** rose while wages lagged.
- Drought or hail could cause a **subsistence crisis** — when basic means of livelihood are endangered.

steps.title: New ideas: the philosophers
steps.body:
A growing **middle class** (merchants, manufacturers, lawyers, administrators) was educated and believed that position should depend on **merit**, not birth.
- **John Locke** (*Two Treatises of Government*) rejected the divine and absolute right of the monarch.
- **Jean-Jacques Rousseau** (*The Social Contract*) proposed government based on a contract between people and their representatives.
- **Montesquieu** (*The Spirit of the Laws*) proposed dividing power among the **legislative, executive and judiciary**.

The American Constitution and its guarantee of individual rights inspired French thinkers. Ideas spread through salons, coffee houses, books and newspapers read aloud.

steps.title: How to answer 'causes' questions
steps.body:
Group causes under headings for full marks:
1. **Social** — privileges of the first two estates.
2. **Economic** — empty treasury, taxes, rising bread prices, subsistence crisis.
3. **Political** — absolute monarchy, Estates-General not called since 1614.
4. **Intellectual** — Locke, Rousseau, Montesquieu; the American example.
Give one specific fact for each.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the Third Estate was only poor peasants. It included rich merchants and lawyers too.
- Mixing up Rousseau (social contract) and Montesquieu (separation of powers).
- Confusing the tithe (to the Church) with the taille (to the state).

lessons.title: 1789: the outbreak and a constitutional monarchy

scenes.text: Versailles, 5 May 1789. The Estates-General meets for the first time since 1614. Each estate is to have one vote.
The Third Estate demands one vote per member. Refused, its members walk out.
On 20 June they gather in an indoor tennis court and swear not to disperse until they have given France a constitution.
On 14 July, crowds in Paris storm the Bastille, a hated fortress-prison. The Revolution has begun.

steps.title: From Estates-General to National Assembly
steps.body: Louis XVI called the **Estates-General** on **5 May 1789** to approve new taxes. Traditionally each estate had **one vote**. The Third Estate demanded voting by head (each member one vote), a democratic principle from Rousseau. When the king refused, its representatives declared themselves the **National Assembly** and took the **Tennis Court Oath (20 June 1789)**, led by **Mirabeau** (a noble) and **Abbé Sieyès** (a priest).

steps.title: Bastille and the Great Fear
steps.body:
- **14 July 1789**: an agitated crowd stormed and destroyed the **Bastille**, a symbol of the king's despotic power.
- In the countryside, rumours spread that lords had hired bands to destroy crops. In a panic called the **Great Fear**, peasants attacked châteaux and burnt documents recording feudal dues.
- On **4 August 1789**, the Assembly **abolished feudal obligations and taxes**; clergy lost tithes, Church lands were confiscated.

steps.title: Constitution of 1791 and the Rights of Man
steps.body:
The Assembly completed a constitution in **1791**: France became a **constitutional monarchy**. Powers were separated and given to an elected **Legislative Assembly**.
- Only men above 25 who paid taxes equal to at least 3 days of a labourer's wage were **active citizens** with the vote. Women, children and men without property were **passive citizens**.

The **Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen** (August 1789) proclaimed rights such as **life, freedom of speech and opinion, equality before law** as 'natural and inalienable'. Symbols: the **broken chain** (freedom), **red Phrygian cap** (liberty), the **blue-white-red tricolour**, the **eye within a triangle radiating light** (knowledge, the eye of the law).

steps.title: Connecting to today
steps.body: Ideas from the Declaration — equality before law, freedom of expression, government by consent — appear in many later documents, including the **Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)** and the Fundamental Rights in **India's Constitution**. Notice how 1791 still excluded women and the poor from voting; universal adult franchise came much later.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying France became a republic in 1789 or 1791. It became a constitutional monarchy in 1791; the Republic came in 1792.
- Saying the 1791 constitution gave everyone the vote — only 'active citizens' (some tax-paying men over 25) could vote.

lessons.title: Republic, Terror, Napoleon and the legacy

scenes.text: In 1791, writer Olympe de Gouges publishes a Declaration of the Rights of Woman and Citizen, arguing women deserve the same rights as men.
During the Reign of Terror she is executed in 1793 for criticising the government.
Women's clubs keep demanding equal political rights. In France, women finally win the vote in 1946.
Today, student Aisha in Hyderabad and student Claire in Lyon debate: did the Revolution keep its promise of equality?

steps.title: War and the Republic
steps.body:
- Neighbouring monarchs feared the Revolution. In **April 1792**, France declared war on **Prussia and Austria**. Volunteers sang the **Marseillaise** (by Roget de L'Isle), now the national anthem.
- Political clubs grew; the most successful were the **Jacobins**, led by **Maximilian Robespierre**. Many members wore long striped trousers like dock workers — called **sans-culottes** ('without knee breeches').
- In **August 1792** Jacobins stormed the Tuileries palace. Elections were held with all men above 21 voting; the new assembly, the **Convention**, abolished the monarchy and declared France a **Republic on 21 September 1792**.
- Louis XVI was tried for treason and executed in **January 1793**; Queen Marie Antoinette later the same year.

steps.title: The Reign of Terror (1793–1794)
steps.body: Robespierre's government followed severe control and punishment. 'Enemies' of the Republic — nobles, clergy, members of other parties, even Jacobins who disagreed — were arrested, tried and **guillotined**. Wages and prices were capped; meat and bread rationed; everyone had to eat 'equality bread'. Churches were converted into barracks. Robespierre's policies became so extreme that he was convicted and executed in **July 1794**.

steps.title: The Directory and Napoleon
steps.body: After 1794, a new constitution denied the vote to non-propertied people; an executive of **five members, the Directory**, was set up to avoid one-man rule. Clashes made it unstable, opening the way for a military dictator, **Napoleon Bonaparte**, who crowned himself **Emperor in 1804**. He conquered much of Europe and introduced laws protecting private property, uniform weights and measures (decimal system), but his armies came to be seen as invaders. He was finally defeated at **Waterloo in 1815**.

steps.title: Women, slavery and legacy
steps.body:
- **Women**: active in clubs and newspapers; some laws improved their lives (state schools, divorce allowed, could train for jobs), but they did not get political rights. Vote came in **1946**.
- **Slavery**: the Convention **abolished slavery in French colonies in 1794**; Napoleon **reintroduced** it; it was finally abolished in **1848**.
- **Everyday life**: censorship was abolished in 1789; newspapers, pamphlets and plays spread new ideas.
- **Legacy**: the ideas of **liberty, equality and democratic rights** spread across Europe in the 19th century and inspired anti-colonial movements; in India, **Tipu Sultan** and **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** are cited as responding to these ideas.

steps.body:
- Saying slavery ended permanently in 1794. It was reintroduced by Napoleon and finally ended in 1848.
- Thinking the Directory was one person. It was five.
- Mixing up Jacobins (Robespierre) and the Directory.

lessons.title: Nationalism in India: satyagraha and Non-Cooperation

scenes.text: 13 April 1919. Families from villages near Amritsar gather in an enclosed ground, Jallianwala Bagh, for the Baisakhi fair; many are unaware martial law has been imposed.
General Dyer blocks the exits and orders troops to fire. Hundreds are killed.
Across India, anger spreads. A young student, Harnam, decides he can no longer attend a British-run college.
Mahatma Gandhi calls for a different kind of struggle — non-violent, mass non-cooperation.

steps.title: The First World War and India
steps.body: The **First World War (1914–18)** created a new economic and political situation: huge defence spending, increased taxes, customs duties raised, income tax introduced, prices doubled between 1913 and 1918; forced recruitment of soldiers in villages; crop failures and an influenza epidemic in 1918–19 killed millions. People's hardships made them receptive to new movements.

steps.title: Gandhi and satyagraha
steps.body:
Gandhi returned from **South Africa in January 1915**. **Satyagraha** stresses the power of **truth** and non-violence: appeal to the conscience of the oppressor rather than use force.
- **Champaran (Bihar), 1917**: against the oppressive indigo plantation system.
- **Kheda (Gujarat), 1917**: peasants affected by crop failure and plague, demanding relaxation of revenue.
- **Ahmedabad, 1918**: cotton mill workers.
- **Rowlatt Act (1919)**: allowed detention of political prisoners without trial for two years. Gandhi launched a nationwide satyagraha (hartal on 6 April 1919).
- **Jallianwala Bagh, 13 April 1919**: massacre by General Dyer's troops in Amritsar.

steps.title: Khilafat and Non-Cooperation
steps.body:
After the defeat of Ottoman Turkey, a harsh treaty was feared for its emperor, the spiritual head of Muslims (the Khalifa). The **Ali brothers, Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali**, began a **Khilafat Movement**. Gandhi saw a chance to unite Hindus and Muslims.

At the **Calcutta session (September 1920)** Gandhi convinced Congress to start **Non-Cooperation**, adopted at the **Nagpur session (December 1920)**. Gandhi's *Hind Swaraj* (1909) argued British rule survived because of Indians' cooperation.

Stages: surrender titles; boycott civil services, army, police, courts, legislative councils, schools and **foreign goods**. In cities, students left government schools, lawyers gave up practice, foreign cloth was burnt in bonfires. Imports of foreign cloth halved between 1921 and 1922.

steps.title: Different strands
steps.body:
- **Awadh peasants** (led by **Baba Ramchandra**): against landlords and high rents; Kisan Sabha formed.
- **Gudem Hills, Andhra Pradesh**: **Alluri Sitarama Raju** led guerrilla resistance by tribals when forests were closed to them.
- **Plantation workers in Assam**: under the **Inland Emigration Act of 1859** they could not leave the tea gardens without permission; many left believing 'Gandhi Raj' was coming.
Each group understood 'swaraj' in its own way.

**Withdrawal**: in **February 1922**, after a violent clash at **Chauri Chaura** (Gorakhpur) in which police were killed, Gandhi called off the movement, feeling people needed training in non-violence. Some leaders (C.R. Das, Motilal Nehru) formed the **Swaraj Party** to contest council elections.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dating the Non-Cooperation Movement to 1930 (that was Civil Disobedience).
- Forgetting that the movement slowed in cities partly because khadi was expensive and alternative Indian institutions were few.
- Saying Gandhi led the Khilafat Movement alone — the Ali brothers began it.

lessons.title: Salt March, Civil Disobedience and a sense of belonging

story.title: A pinch of salt at Dandi

scenes.text: 12 March 1930. Gandhi, then 60, sets out from Sabarmati Ashram with 78 volunteers, walking about 240 miles to the coastal village of Dandi.
On 6 April 1930, he picks up salt made by boiling seawater — breaking the colonial salt law.
Salt was eaten by rich and poor alike. A tax on it hurt everyone, so everyone understood the protest.
Newspapers around the world carry the story. Leela, a girl in Bombay, joins women picketing liquor shops.

steps.title: The road to Purna Swaraj
steps.body:
- **Simon Commission** (1928): had no Indian member; greeted with 'Go back, Simon'.
- **Lord Irwin** offered vague 'dominion status' (1929) and a Round Table Conference.
- At the **Lahore Congress (December 1929)**, under **Jawaharlal Nehru**, the demand for **Purna Swaraj** (complete independence) was formalised. **26 January 1930** was celebrated as Independence Day.

steps.title: Salt March and Civil Disobedience
steps.body:
On 31 January 1930 Gandhi sent Irwin **eleven demands**; the most stirring was to **abolish the salt tax**. When ignored, he began the **Salt March (12 March – 6 April 1930)** to Dandi.

**Civil Disobedience** differed from Non-Cooperation: people were asked not only to refuse cooperation but to **break colonial laws** — making salt, boycotting foreign cloth, picketing liquor shops, refusing to pay revenue and taxes, violating forest laws.

The British arrested leaders; brutal repression followed. Gandhi called off the movement and signed the **Gandhi–Irwin Pact (5 March 1931)**, then attended the **Second Round Table Conference** in London (December 1931), which failed. The movement was relaunched but lost momentum by 1934.

steps.title: Who joined, and why
steps.body:
- **Rich peasants** (Patidars of Gujarat, Jats of UP): hit by falling prices in the Depression; wanted revenue reduced.
- **Poor peasants**: wanted rents to landlords remitted — Congress was reluctant to support 'no rent' campaigns.
- **Business classes** (Purshottamdas Thakurdas, G.D. Birla): wanted protection against imports; formed FICCI (1927).
- **Industrial workers**: some joined selectively (e.g. Nagpur).
- **Women**: participated in large numbers — marching, making salt, picketing.

**Limits**: many **Dalits** ('depressed classes') sought separate electorates. **Dr B.R. Ambedkar** organised them; after Gandhi's fast, the **Poona Pact (September 1932)** gave reserved seats in councils, voted by the general electorate. Many **Muslims** felt alienated after the decline of Khilafat and the failure of talks on representation.

steps.title: A sense of collective belonging
steps.body:
Nationalism also grew through culture:
- The image of **Bharat Mata** — first created by **Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay**, who wrote **'Vande Mataram'** in the 1870s; painted famously by **Abanindranath Tagore**.
- Collection of **folklore** (Rabindranath Tagore in Bengal; Natesa Sastri's folklore of southern India).
- **Flags**: the Swadeshi tricolour (red, green, yellow) in Bengal; Gandhi's tricolour with the spinning wheel by 1921.
- **Reinterpreting history**: writers recalled India's achievements in art, science and mathematics to counter colonial claims.

Such symbols united many, but some groups felt left out — a reminder that nationalism must include everyone.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing the Poona Pact (1932, Gandhi–Ambedkar) with the Gandhi–Irwin Pact (1931).
- Saying Civil Disobedience only meant boycott — its key feature was **breaking laws**.
- Forgetting that 26 January 1930 was the first 'Independence Day'; the Constitution later came into force on 26 January 1950 to honour it.

lessons.title: Resources and sustainable development

story.title: The village that planned its water

scenes.text: Ralegan Siddhi in Maharashtra once faced severe drought and poverty.
From the 1970s, villagers led by social worker Anna Hazare built check dams, planted trees and managed grazing together.
Groundwater rose, crops returned and the village became a widely studied example of community resource management.
Students in Kenya study similar community projects. Resources are not just found — they are planned and cared for.

steps.title: What is a resource?
steps.body: Anything in our environment that can satisfy our needs, is **technologically accessible**, **economically feasible** and **culturally acceptable** is a resource. Resources are created by the interaction of nature, technology and human institutions — human beings themselves are an essential part of this.

steps.title: Classifying resources
steps.body:
- **Origin**: biotic (living — plants, animals, humans) and abiotic (non-living — rocks, metals).
- **Exhaustibility**: **renewable** (solar, wind, water, forests — can be renewed) and **non-renewable** (fossil fuels, minerals — take millions of years to form; some like metals are recyclable).
- **Ownership**: individual, community, national, international (e.g. oceanic resources beyond 200 nautical miles of the Exclusive Economic Zone belong to the open ocean and are governed internationally).
- **Status of development**: potential (found but not used — e.g. Rajasthan and Gujarat's wind and solar potential), developed, **stock** (we lack technology to use them, e.g. hydrogen from water as fuel), and **reserves** (subset of stock usable with existing technology, kept for future).

steps.title: Sustainable development and the Earth Summit
steps.body:
**Sustainable development**: development that meets present needs without damaging the environment and without compromising the needs of future generations.

**Rio de Janeiro Earth Summit (1992)**: world leaders signed declarations on climate change and biodiversity and adopted **Agenda 21**, aimed at combating environmental damage, poverty and disease through global cooperation, with every local government encouraged to draw its own local Agenda 21.

Mahatma Gandhi summed it up: 'There is enough for everybody's need and not for anybody's greed.'

steps.title: Resource planning in India
steps.body:
India has huge diversity in resource availability: Jharkhand is rich in minerals and coal; Arunachal Pradesh has abundant water but lacks infrastructure; Rajasthan has solar and wind potential but limited water.

**Steps**: (1) identify and inventory resources (survey, mapping, estimating); (2) build a planning structure with suitable technology, skills and institutions; (3) match resource plans with overall national development plans.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling all metals non-renewable and non-recyclable. Metals are non-renewable but recyclable.
- Confusing **stock** (no technology yet) with **reserves** (usable now, saved for future).

lessons.title: Land and soils of India

scenes.text: Shankar grows cotton near Akola in Maharashtra's Vidarbha region on dark, sticky soil his family calls 'kali mitti'.
In summer, deep cracks appear in the fields — good for aeration, his father explains.
His cousin Anjali in Kerala grows cashew on reddish laterite soil that needs lots of manure.
India's soils are as diverse as its people.

steps.title: Land as a resource
steps.body:
Land is used for forests, agriculture, settlements, roads and industry. India's land has mountains (about 30%), plateaus (about 27%) and plains (about 43%). Some land is **waste land** (rocky, arid, deserts) or **fallow** (left uncultivated for some time to regain fertility).

**Land degradation** causes: deforestation, overgrazing, mining (Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, MP, Odisha), over-irrigation leading to waterlogging and salinity (Punjab, Haryana, western UP), and dust from industries like cement and stone grinding.

steps.title: Major soil types
steps.body:
- **Alluvial**: most widespread; deposited by Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra systems across the northern plains (also in eastern coastal deltas). Very fertile; **khadar** (new, finer) and **bangar** (old, with kankar nodules). Good for sugarcane, paddy, wheat, pulses.
- **Black (regur)**: formed from lava (Deccan trap) rocks; Maharashtra, Saurashtra, Malwa, MP, Chhattisgarh. Clayey, holds moisture, rich in calcium, potash, magnesium; develops deep **cracks** in the hot season. Ideal for **cotton**.
- **Red and yellow**: on crystalline igneous rocks of the Deccan plateau's eastern and southern parts; red due to iron diffusion, yellow when hydrated.
- **Laterite**: high temperature and heavy rainfall cause intense **leaching**; low in humus. With manure and fertiliser, useful for **cashew**, tea and coffee (Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu hills).
- **Arid**: sandy, saline, red to brown; Rajasthan; low humus and moisture; kankar layer below. Can be cultivated with irrigation, as in western Rajasthan.
- **Forest**: in hills and mountains; varies in texture; acidic and low in humus on snow-covered peaks.

steps.title: Soil erosion and conservation
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying laterite soil is very fertile naturally. It is leached and needs manure.
- Mixing khadar (new alluvium) and bangar (old alluvium).
- Saying black soil is from rivers. It is formed from volcanic (lava) rocks.

lessons.title: Water resources: dams and rainwater harvesting

scenes.text: In Phalodi, Rajasthan, Kamla's family house has an underground tank called a tanka beneath the courtyard.
Rain from the rooftop flows through pipes into it, stored for months.
In the hot summer, the tanka water stays cool. The family calls it 'palar pani' — the purest form of natural water.
Old wisdom, modern relevance: today many Indian cities require rooftop rainwater harvesting.

steps.title: Water scarcity
steps.body: About three-quarters of Earth is covered by water, but only a small fraction is usable fresh water. Water scarcity can be caused not just by low rainfall but by **over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access** — growing population, intensive irrigation (especially for water-hungry crops), industrialisation and urbanisation, and **pollution** by domestic and industrial waste.

steps.title: Multipurpose river projects
steps.body:
Dams are built for irrigation, electricity, water supply, flood control, fish breeding, recreation and navigation. Jawaharlal Nehru called them the '**temples of modern India**'. Examples: **Bhakra Nangal** (Sutlej–Beas) for hydel power and irrigation; **Hirakud** (Mahanadi) for flood control and irrigation.

**Criticisms**: regulating rivers affects natural flow and sediment, harms aquatic life, submerges forests and farmland, displaces local communities, and may cause new problems like waterlogging. Movements such as the **Narmada Bachao Andolan** raised issues of rehabilitation and the environment in the Sardar Sarovar project. Disputes between states over water-sharing are also common.

steps.title: Rainwater harvesting traditions
steps.body:
- **Guls / kuls**: diversion channels in the Western Himalayas.
- **Rooftop harvesting** in Rajasthan (**tankas**), and in Shillong, Meghalaya — despite nearby Cherrapunji–Mawsynram being among the wettest places, many homes in Shillong harvest rooftop water.
- **Khadins** in Jaisalmer and **johads** in other parts of Rajasthan: rain-fed storage on agricultural fields.
- **Inundation channels** in Bengal floodplains.
- **Bamboo drip irrigation** in Meghalaya: water from springs is carried through bamboo pipes down the hill.
- **Tamil Nadu** was the first state to make rooftop rainwater harvesting **compulsory** for all houses.

steps.title: You can save water
steps.body:
- Fix leaking taps (a slow drip can waste many litres a day).
- Use a bucket instead of a hose to wash vehicles.
- Reuse RO-reject water for mopping or plants.
- Ask your housing society or school about rainwater harvesting.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking water scarcity happens only in dry regions. Cities with good rainfall also face it due to overuse and pollution.
- Writing only advantages of dams — board questions often ask for **both** sides.

lessons.title: Agriculture

scenes.text: In Ludhiana, Harpreet's family sows paddy when the monsoon arrives in June — the kharif crop.
In October–November, after harvesting paddy, they sow wheat — the rabi crop — harvested in April.
In the short summer gap, they grow watermelons and fodder — the zaid season.
Harpreet checks the minimum support price on her phone before the harvest is sold.

steps.title: Types of farming
steps.body:
- **Primitive subsistence farming**: on small patches with simple tools (hoe, dao, digging sticks) and family labour. **Slash and burn ('jhumming')** in the north-east; a patch is cleared, cultivated, then left to recover.
- **Intensive subsistence farming**: in densely populated areas; high use of biochemical inputs and irrigation on small holdings.
- **Commercial farming**: high-yielding varieties, fertilisers, pesticides, machines; for sale. Rice is commercial in Punjab and Haryana but subsistence in parts of Odisha.
- **Plantation**: a single crop on a large area with lots of capital and labour — tea, coffee, rubber, sugarcane, banana; linked to industries.

steps.title: Cropping seasons
steps.body:
- **Rabi**: sown in winter (October–December), harvested in summer (April–June). Wheat, barley, peas, gram, mustard. Western temperate cyclones bring winter rain that helps. Punjab, Haryana, HP, J&K, Uttarakhand, UP are important.
- **Kharif**: sown with the onset of monsoon, harvested in September–October. Paddy, maize, jowar, bajra, tur (arhar), moong, urad, cotton, jute, groundnut, soybean. Assam, West Bengal and coastal Odisha may grow three paddy crops a year (aus, aman, boro).
- **Zaid**: short summer season between rabi and kharif — watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables, fodder crops.

steps.title: Conditions for major crops
steps.body:
- **Rice**: high temperature (above 25 °C), high humidity, rainfall above 100 cm (or irrigation). India is the **second largest producer** (after China).
- **Wheat**: cool growing season, bright sunshine at ripening, 50–75 cm rainfall evenly spread. Ganga–Satluj plains and the black soil region of the Deccan.
- **Millets** (jowar, bajra, ragi): hardy; grow on less fertile and sandy soils; very nutritious (ragi is rich in iron, calcium and fibre).
- **Pulses**: India is the **largest producer and consumer** of pulses; legumes (except arhar) fix nitrogen, restoring soil fertility, so they are rotated with other crops.
- **Sugarcane**: tropical/subtropical, 21–27 °C, 75–100 cm rain.
- **Tea**: warm, moist, frost-free climate, well-drained soils, frequent showers; labour-intensive (Assam, Darjeeling, Nilgiris).
- **Cotton**: black soil of the Deccan; high temperature, light rainfall, 210 frost-free days, bright sunshine; kharif crop.

steps.title: Technological and institutional reforms
steps.body:
- **Green Revolution** (from the 1960s): high-yielding seeds, fertilisers, irrigation — big rise in wheat and rice output, especially in Punjab and Haryana.
- **White Revolution (Operation Flood)**: dairy cooperatives raised milk production.
- Land reforms: abolition of zamindari, consolidation of holdings. **Bhoodan–Gramdan** (land gift) movement of **Vinoba Bhave**.
- Schemes: **Minimum Support Price (MSP)** announced for crops, **Kisan Credit Card (KCC)**, crop insurance, weather and crop information on radio and TV, rural banks and cooperatives.

Challenges today: small landholdings, debt, falling groundwater, price fluctuations, climate change, and the need for diversification (horticulture, fisheries, organic farming).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing rabi and kharif: **R**abi = **R**eaped in spring (sown in winter); kharif = monsoon-sown.
- Saying wheat needs heavy rainfall — it needs moderate rain (50–75 cm).
- Calling tea a rabi crop. It is a plantation crop.
