lessons.title: What is democracy? Why democracy?

scenes.text: In a school in Bhopal, the principal suddenly appoints Aman as class monitor for the whole year.
Students complain: 'We never chose him, and we can't remove him!'
Their teacher, Mrs. Qureshi, proposes an election: each student one vote, a new vote every term, rules everyone follows.
'Now you've discovered the key features of democracy,' she smiles.

steps.title: A simple definition
steps.body:
**Democracy** is a form of government in which **the rulers are elected by the people**. But not every country with elections is a democracy. Four features make the definition complete:
1. **Major decisions are taken by elected leaders** (not, say, the army behind the scenes).
2. **Free and fair electoral competition**: people have a real choice and can change rulers.
3. **One person, one vote, one value**: every adult citizen has one vote, and each vote has equal value.
4. **Rule of law and respect for rights**: a democratic government works within constitutional law and protects citizens' rights.

steps.title: Examples from around the world
steps.body:
- When rulers are not elected but take power by force (military coups), it is not a democracy.
- When elections are held but only one party is allowed, or the main opposition is suppressed, the choice is not real.
- When some groups are denied the vote (for example, women in some countries in the past), it is not 'one person, one vote'.
- When courts are not independent or rights can be ignored, the rule of law is weak.

The word comes from Greek *demos* (people) and *kratia* (rule).

steps.title: Arguments for and against
Broader meanings
steps.body: Democracy also applies to everyday life: a family where decisions are discussed, a school council, a housing society that votes on budgets. A democratic decision involves **consultation and consent** of all affected, with even the weakest having a voice.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking elections alone make a democracy. They must be **free and fair**, and rights must be protected.
- Saying democracy guarantees economic prosperity. It provides the means; outcomes depend on policies and people.

lessons.title: Constitutional design: making India's Constitution

scenes.text: From December 1946, about 300 members of the Constituent Assembly meet in Delhi to write India's Constitution.
They debate for nearly three years, clause by clause — on rights, language, federalism and more.
Dr B.R. Ambedkar chairs the Drafting Committee. Members include women like Hansa Mehta and Durgabai Deshmukh.
On 26 November 1949 the Constitution is adopted; on 26 January 1950 it comes into force. Today Ishaan reads its Preamble at school assembly.

steps.title: Why do we need a constitution?
steps.body:
A **constitution** is a set of written rules accepted by all people living together in a country. It is the supreme law that:
- generates trust and coordination among different groups,
- specifies how the government will be constituted and who takes which decisions,
- **limits the powers** of government and tells us citizens' **rights**,
- expresses the aspirations of people about creating a good society.

South Africa's 1996 constitution, written after the end of **apartheid** (racial segregation), is a powerful example of a constitution creating trust between former oppressors and oppressed. Nelson Mandela became its first president elected under universal franchise (1994).

steps.title: Making the Indian Constitution
steps.body:
- The **Constituent Assembly** was elected mainly by members of provincial legislatures; its first meeting was in **December 1946**. After Partition it was divided; India's Assembly had **299 members**.
- **Dr Rajendra Prasad** was its President; **Dr B.R. Ambedkar** chaired the **Drafting Committee**.
- Adopted on **26 November 1949** (now observed as **Constitution Day**); came into force on **26 January 1950** (**Republic Day**).
- It drew on the national movement's experience (e.g. the 1928 Motilal Nehru draft and the 1931 Karachi resolution on fundamental rights) and studied other constitutions, while being shaped by Indian needs.
- It is one of the world's longest written constitutions and has been amended many times.

steps.title: Values in the Preamble
steps.body:
'**We, the people of India**' — the Constitution is made by the people themselves.
- **Sovereign**: people have supreme right to decide; no external power can dictate.
- **Socialist**: wealth generated socially should be shared equally; government should reduce inequalities.
- **Secular**: no official religion; freedom to follow any religion.
- **Democratic**: people enjoy equal political rights, elect rulers and hold them accountable.
- **Republic**: head of state is elected, not hereditary.
- **Justice** (social, economic, political), **Liberty** (of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship), **Equality** (of status and opportunity), **Fraternity** (sense of brotherhood and sisterhood, dignity of the individual, unity and integrity of the nation).

'Socialist' and 'secular' were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing 26 November 1949 (adoption) with 26 January 1950 (came into force).
- Saying Ambedkar was President of the Constituent Assembly — he chaired the Drafting Committee; Rajendra Prasad was President.
- Thinking a constitution cannot change. India's can be amended through a set procedure; some basic features cannot be destroyed (as interpreted by the Supreme Court).

lessons.title: Electoral politics: how elections work

scenes.text: Ninety-year-old Savitri Devi in Varanasi has voted in many general elections — first with paper ballots, now with an EVM.
Her granddaughter Pooja, who just turned 18, votes for the first time. An official marks her finger with indelible ink.
Pooja presses a button and sees a VVPAT slip confirming her choice for a few seconds.
'Your vote counts exactly as much as the Prime Minister's,' Savitri Devi tells her proudly.

steps.title: Why elections?
steps.body: In a large democracy, people choose **representatives**. Elections let voters choose who makes laws, who forms the government, and which party's policies guide it. An election is **democratic** only if: everyone can choose (universal adult franchise); there are parties and candidates to choose from; elections happen at **regular intervals**; the candidate preferred by the people wins; and the process is **free and fair**.

steps.title: India's electoral system
steps.body:
- **Lok Sabha**: India is divided into **543 constituencies**; each elects one Member of Parliament (MP). State assemblies have their own constituencies electing MLAs.
- **First-past-the-post**: the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins.
- **Reserved constituencies**: some seats are reserved for **Scheduled Castes (SC)** and **Scheduled Tribes (ST)**; in local bodies, seats are also reserved for OBCs and **one-third for women**. The **106th Constitutional Amendment (2023)** provides one-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies, to take effect after the next census and delimitation.
- **Voting age**: **18 years** (lowered from 21 by the 61st Amendment, 1988). Voters must be on the **electoral roll** and carry an Elector's Photo Identity Card (EPIC) or other permitted ID.
- Anyone who can vote can contest (minimum age 25 for Lok Sabha and state assemblies).

steps.title: Election Commission and campaigns
steps.body:
The **Election Commission of India** is an independent body that conducts elections: it implements the **Model Code of Conduct**, orders re-polls, and controls government officials on election duty. Since 2013, voters can choose **NOTA** ('None of the Above').

Campaign rules forbid bribing or threatening voters, appealing on the basis of caste or religion, using government resources for campaigns, and spending above legal limits. **Candidates must declare** criminal cases, assets and educational qualifications in a legal affidavit.

steps.title: Challenges to free and fair elections
steps.body:
- Candidates with huge money power have unfair advantages.
- Some candidates with criminal backgrounds get tickets.
- Some families dominate parties.
- Voters sometimes have little real choice between major parties.
- Smaller parties and independents face disadvantages.

Citizens, the media and the Election Commission help address these. Turnout in India is high, and poorer and less-educated people often vote in larger proportions than the rich — a sign of faith in democracy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the government in power conducts elections. The independent **Election Commission** does.
- Thinking reserved constituencies mean only SC/ST people can vote there. Everyone votes; only the candidates must belong to the reserved group.

lessons.title: Power sharing and federalism

scenes.text: In Belgium, Dutch-speakers, French-speakers and a small German-speaking group live together. Tension rose in the 1950s–60s.
Belgium chose to share power: between 1970 and 1993 it amended its constitution four times to give every community a voice.
Sri Lanka chose majority dominance after independence in 1948, with Sinhala declared the only official language in 1956. Distrust grew into a long civil war.
Student Riya in Bengaluru and student Pieter in Brussels compare notes: sharing power keeps a diverse country together.

steps.title: Belgium and Sri Lanka
steps.body:
**Belgium**: about 59% Dutch-speaking (Flemish region), 40% French-speaking (Wallonia), 1% German-speaking. In Brussels, the capital, about 80% spoke French and 20% Dutch. Arrangements: equal number of Dutch- and French-speaking ministers in the central government; powers given to state governments; Brussels has its own government with equal representation; a '**community government**' elected by each language community handles cultural, educational and language issues.

**Sri Lanka**: Sinhala-speakers about 74%, Tamil-speakers about 18%. The **1956 Act** made **Sinhala the only official language**; preferential policies for Sinhala applicants in universities and government jobs; Buddhism protected by the state. Sri Lankan Tamils felt alienated; demands for autonomy turned into a **civil war** that ended in 2009.

**Lesson**: majoritarianism undermines unity; accommodation strengthens it.

steps.title: Why share power, and how
steps.body:
**Prudential reason**: power sharing reduces conflict between social groups and ensures political stability. **Moral reason**: it is the very spirit of democracy — people affected by policies should have a say.

**Forms**:
1. **Horizontal**: among organs of government — legislature, executive, judiciary (checks and balances).
2. **Vertical**: among levels of government — union, state, local.
3. **Among social groups**: e.g. reserved constituencies, community government.
4. **Among parties, pressure groups and movements**: coalition governments, interest groups influencing decisions.

steps.title: Federalism in India
steps.body:
**Federalism**: power divided between a central authority and constituent units. India is a 'holding together' federation.

The Constitution's three lists:
- **Union List**: defence, foreign affairs, banking, currency — Parliament legislates.
- **State List**: police, trade within the state, agriculture, irrigation.
- **Concurrent List**: education, forests, marriage, adoption, trade unions — both can legislate; if they conflict, **Union law prevails**.
- Subjects not in any list (**residuary**, e.g. computer software) go to the Union.

The judiciary settles disputes. States were reorganised on linguistic lines (from 1956) — this strengthened unity. India's language policy: no single national language; Hindi is an official language with English, and the 8th Schedule lists 22 languages.

steps.title: Local self-government (third tier)
steps.body:
The **73rd and 74th Amendments (1992)** made local government a third tier:
- Regular elections mandatory, conducted by **State Election Commissions**.
- Seats reserved for SC, ST and OBC.
- At least **one-third of seats reserved for women** (many states now reserve 50%).
- States must share some powers and revenue with local bodies.

Rural: **Gram Panchayat** (headed by sarpanch/pradhan) → **Panchayat Samiti** (block) → **Zila Parishad** (district). The **Gram Sabha** (all voters of the village) reviews the panchayat's work. Urban: municipalities and municipal corporations (headed by a mayor).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Sri Lanka adopted power sharing in 1956 — it did the opposite.
- Putting police in the Union List (it's in the State List) or education in the State List (it's in the Concurrent List).
- Confusing horizontal (organs) and vertical (levels) power sharing.

lessons.title: Development: goals and measures

story.title: What does development mean to you?

scenes.text: A landless labourer in rural Bihar, Ramesh, wants more days of work, better wages and a good school for his children.
A software engineer in Pune, Shreya, wants safe roads at night and equal pay with her male colleagues.
An adivasi elder in Jharkhand, Somra, fears a new mine will destroy the forest his people depend on.
Same country, different goals. Development means different things — and sometimes they conflict.

steps.title: Different goals, conflicting goals
steps.body:
People have **different development goals** depending on their situation. What is development for one may not be for another — a dam may give electricity to cities but displace villagers.

People seek not only more income but also **equal treatment, freedom, security, respect** and a safe environment. **Non-material** things matter, not only money.

steps.title: Income as a measure
steps.body:
**Per capita income** (average income) = total income of the country / total population. The **World Bank** uses it to classify countries (high-income, middle-income, low-income).

**Limitation**: averages hide **inequality**. Two countries with the same average income may differ widely — in one, most people have similar incomes; in another, a few are very rich and most are poor.

steps.title: Beyond income: health, education, HDI
steps.body:
- **Infant Mortality Rate (IMR)**: deaths of children under 1 year per 1000 live births.
- **Literacy rate**: proportion of literate population aged 7 and above.
- **Net attendance ratio**: children of age 14–15 attending school as a percentage of all children of that age.

NCERT's comparison shows Kerala, with lower per capita income than some richer states, had lower IMR and higher literacy — because of good public health and education facilities and a strong Public Distribution System.

**Human Development Index (HDI)**, published by the **UNDP** in the Human Development Report, combines **income, health (life expectancy) and education**.

steps.title: Sustainability of development
steps.body: Development must be **sustainable**. Groundwater over-use (many districts in India face falling water tables), and dependence on **non-renewable** resources like crude oil, threaten future generations. Environmental consequences cross state and national boundaries — sustainability is everyone's concern.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a higher average income always means a better life for everyone.
- Confusing IMR with birth rate.
- Forgetting that HDI includes three dimensions (income, health, education).

lessons.title: Sectors of the Indian economy

scenes.text: In Gujarat, farmer Kantibhai grows cotton — the primary sector.
A mill in Tiruppur spins it into yarn and weaves T-shirts — the secondary sector.
Trucks transport the shirts, a bank lends money to the shop, and a shopkeeper in Delhi sells them — the tertiary sector.
When Ritu buys a T-shirt, she is the final link in a chain connecting all three sectors.

steps.title: Three sectors
steps.body:
- **Primary (agriculture and related)**: directly using natural resources — farming, dairy, fishing, forestry, mining.
- **Secondary (industrial)**: natural products changed into other forms through manufacturing — cotton → cloth, sugarcane → sugar, building construction.
- **Tertiary (service)**: activities that support the other two — transport, storage, communication, banking, trade; also teachers, doctors, IT services.

**GDP (Gross Domestic Product)**: value of all **final goods and services** produced within a country in a year. Only final goods are counted to avoid double counting (the value of wheat is already included in the price of biscuits).

steps.title: Changing importance
steps.body:
In most developed countries, the tertiary sector is now the largest. In India too, the **tertiary sector** has become the largest producing sector in GDP terms. But **employment** has not shifted as much — a large share of workers is still in the primary sector, many with **disguised unemployment** (more people working than needed; if some leave, output doesn't fall).

Ways to create jobs: better irrigation and storage, cheap credit, small-scale industries in semi-rural areas, and expanding education and health services. The **Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) 2005** guarantees **100 days of employment** a year to rural households that seek it; if work is not provided, an unemployment allowance is payable.

steps.title: Organised vs unorganised; public vs private
steps.body:
- **Organised sector**: registered enterprises following rules — regular jobs, fixed hours, paid leave, provident fund, safety.
- **Unorganised sector**: small, scattered units, largely outside government control — low pay, no job security, no paid leave. Many workers in India are in this sector (e.g. construction labourers, street vendors).
- **Public sector**: government owns most assets (railways, post offices) — aims at public welfare.
- **Private sector**: privately owned — aims at profit (Tata Steel, Reliance Industries are examples used in textbooks).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting intermediate goods in GDP (double counting).
- Thinking the tertiary sector employs most Indians — it produces the largest share of GDP, but the primary sector still employs a very large share.
- Thinking 'unorganised' means illegal. It means unregistered and unprotected.

lessons.title: Money and credit

scenes.text: Swapna, a small farmer in Andhra Pradesh, borrows from a local moneylender to grow groundnut, promising to sell her crop to him.
Pests ruin her crop. She cannot repay, and the high interest keeps adding up. She has to sell part of her land.
Her friend Lakshmi joins a women's self-help group, where members save regularly and lend to each other at fair rates.
With the group's help, Lakshmi later gets a bank loan without collateral. Credit can trap you — or set you free.

steps.title: Why money?
steps.body:
Under **barter**, goods are exchanged directly — but you need a **double coincidence of wants** (each person must want what the other has). Money solves this: it is a **medium of exchange**, accepted by all.

Modern money: **currency** (paper notes and coins) and **deposits in banks**. In India, the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** issues currency notes on behalf of the government; the rupee is legal tender — it cannot be refused in settling transactions in India.

**Demand deposits**: deposits that can be withdrawn on demand; cheques and digital payments (UPI, cards) let us pay using them.

steps.title: Banks and credit
steps.body:
Banks keep a small proportion of deposits as cash for withdrawals and use most of the rest to give **loans**. The difference between the interest charged on loans and paid on deposits is their main income.

**Credit (loan)**: an agreement where the lender supplies money, goods or services in return for a promise of future payment. Terms of credit: **interest rate, collateral** (an asset like land, a building or gold, pledged as a guarantee), documentation and mode of repayment.

Credit can **help** (Salim's factory gets loans to meet a big order and earns profit) or create a **debt trap** (Swapna's crop failure).

steps.title: Formal and informal credit
steps.body:
- **Formal**: banks and cooperatives — supervised by the **RBI**, lower interest, regulated terms.
- **Informal**: moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives — no supervision; often very high interest; can demand harsh terms.

Rich households get most credit from formal sources; poor households depend much more on informal sources. So formal credit must expand, and be **distributed more fairly**.

**Self-Help Groups (SHGs)**: usually **15–20 members**, mostly women from one locality, who save regularly and lend to members. After a year or two, the group can get bank loans **without collateral**. SHGs help women become financially self-reliant and discuss social issues. Bangladesh's **Grameen Bank**, founded by **Professor Muhammad Yunus** (Nobel Peace Prize 2006), is a well-known example of credit for the poor.

steps.title: Smart borrowing
steps.body:
- Compare the **annual interest rate**, not just the monthly amount.
- Borrow from regulated lenders; check that apps are RBI-registered or partnered with regulated entities.
- Never share OTPs or passwords. Be wary of instant-loan apps demanding access to your contacts and photos.
- If you get trapped by harassment for a loan, keep records and report it to the police and the cyber-crime helpline 1930.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying banks keep all deposits as cash — they lend most of it.
- Thinking informal credit is always cheaper because it is 'friendly'. It is often far costlier.
- Mixing up collateral (an asset pledged) with interest (the cost of borrowing).

lessons.title: Globalisation and the Indian economy

scenes.text: Arjun in Kochi buys a smartphone. Its design came from one country, its chips from another, and it was assembled in a factory in India.
His sister Neha works for a multinational company, answering customers from the UK and Australia through the internet.
Meanwhile, a small toy-maker in Channapatna worries about cheap imported toys.
Globalisation brings opportunities and challenges — and they are not shared equally.

steps.title: MNCs and production across countries
steps.body:
A **multinational corporation (MNC)** owns or controls production in **more than one country**. MNCs set up production where it is close to markets, where skilled and unskilled labour is available at low cost, and where government policies are favourable.

Ways MNCs spread: setting up factories (an investment called **foreign investment**), **joint ventures** with local companies, **buying up local companies**, and placing **orders with small producers** (garments, footwear, sports items).

steps.title: What is globalisation?
steps.body:
**Globalisation** is the process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries — more **goods and services, investment, technology** and, to some extent, **people** moving across borders. Foreign trade connects markets: consumers get more choice; producers face competition.

**Enablers**: rapid improvement in **technology** — transport (containers), information and communication technology (telecom, computers, internet).

**Liberalisation**: removing barriers or restrictions set by the government. **Trade barriers** like import taxes (tariffs) and quotas protect domestic producers. Around **1991**, India began major economic reforms, reducing barriers on foreign trade and investment.

steps.title: WTO and fairness
steps.body:
The **World Trade Organisation (WTO)** aims to liberalise international trade; it sets rules and has about 160+ member countries. However, developed countries have sometimes retained trade barriers unfairly (for example, large subsidies to their own farmers), while asking developing countries to remove theirs.

**Special Economic Zones (SEZs)** offer world-class facilities and tax benefits to attract foreign companies. Governments have also relaxed some labour laws, raising concerns about job security.

steps.title: Impacts and fair globalisation
steps.body:
**Benefits**: more choice and lower prices for well-off consumers; new jobs in some sectors (IT, services); some Indian companies have become multinationals themselves; new opportunities for service providers.

**Problems**: small producers (batteries, plastics, toys, dairy, vegetable oil) hit by competition; many workers face insecure, temporary jobs with long hours and low wages.

**Fair globalisation** means creating opportunities for all and ensuring benefits are better shared: governments protecting workers' rights, supporting small producers, negotiating fairer WTO rules; people's organisations campaigning for fairness.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying globalisation means only free movement of people. People's movement is still fairly restricted; goods, services and investment move much more freely.
- Saying a company is an MNC just because it exports. An MNC owns or controls **production** in more than one country.

lessons.title: Cells: discovery, types and the cell membrane

scenes.text: Zainab in Srinagar soaks dry raisins in water for her mother's kheer. By morning they are plump.
Her brother sprinkles salt on cut cucumber slices for a salad. Soon water drips out of them.
Opposite effects! Their biology teacher, Ms. Bhat, says: 'Both are osmosis — water moving across cell membranes.'
To understand it, we need to meet the cell — the basic unit of life.

steps.title: Discovery and cell theory
steps.body:
- **Robert Hooke (1665)** saw tiny compartments in a thin slice of cork and named them 'cells'. (He saw dead cell walls.)
- **Leeuwenhoek (1674)** first saw free-living cells in pond water with improved lenses.
- **Robert Brown (1831)** discovered the nucleus.
- **Schleiden (1838) and Schwann (1839)**: all plants and animals are made of cells.
- **Virchow (1855)**: all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

**Cell theory**: all living things are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of structure and function; new cells come from existing cells.

steps.title: Kinds of cells
steps.body:
- **Unicellular** organisms: one cell does everything (Amoeba, Paramecium, bacteria). **Multicellular**: many cells with division of labour (humans, plants).
- **Prokaryotic cells** (bacteria): no true nucleus — the genetic material lies in a region called the **nucleoid** without a membrane; no membrane-bound organelles.
- **Eukaryotic cells** (plants, animals, fungi): a true nucleus with a nuclear membrane, and membrane-bound organelles.

Cells vary: the longest human cells are nerve cells; red blood cells lack a nucleus when mature; an ostrich egg is a single very large cell.

steps.title: Plasma membrane, diffusion and osmosis
steps.body:
The **plasma membrane** is **selectively permeable**: it lets some substances in and out but not others. It is flexible, made of lipids and proteins — so cells can engulf food (**endocytosis**, as in Amoeba).

- **Diffusion**: movement of particles from higher to lower concentration (CO₂ out of cells, O₂ in).
- **Osmosis**: movement of **water** through a selectively permeable membrane from a region of **higher water concentration (dilute solution)** to **lower water concentration (concentrated solution)**.
  - **Hypotonic** outside solution (more dilute) → cell **gains water, swells** (raisins in water).
  - **Isotonic** → no net change.
  - **Hypertonic** (more concentrated) → cell **loses water, shrinks** (salted cucumber). In plant cells, the shrinking of contents away from the wall is **plasmolysis**.

steps.title: Cell wall
steps.body: Plant cells (and fungi, bacteria) have a **cell wall** outside the membrane. In plants it is made mainly of **cellulose**. It gives strength and lets plant cells withstand very dilute surroundings without bursting. Animal cells have no cell wall — an animal cell in pure water may burst.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the cell wall is selectively permeable — it is the **membrane** that is; the plant cell wall is freely permeable.
- Defining osmosis as movement of solute. Osmosis is movement of **water** (solvent).
- Thinking Hooke saw living cells. He saw dead cork cells.

2. Why does a de-shelled egg (shell dissolved in dilute acid) swell in water and shrink in strong salt solution? (Osmosis through its membrane.)

lessons.title: Cell organelles

scenes.text: For a school project in Bhubaneswar, Arpita builds a model 'Cell City' out of cardboard.
The nucleus is City Hall with the blueprints. Mitochondria are power stations.
The endoplasmic reticulum is the road network; the Golgi apparatus is the post office packing parcels.
Lysosomes are the waste-disposal crew. Her friend Mateo from Peru adds solar panels — chloroplasts — for a plant-cell version!

steps.title: Nucleus
steps.body:
The **nucleus** has a double-layered **nuclear membrane** with pores. It contains **chromosomes**, made of **DNA** and proteins, visible as rod-shaped structures during cell division; at other times as a tangled mass called **chromatin**. DNA carries the information for making and organising the cell; functional segments of DNA are **genes**.

The nucleus controls the cell's activities and plays a central role in cell division and inheritance.

steps.title: Membrane-bound organelles
steps.body:
- **Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)**: network of membrane tubes. **Rough ER** has ribosomes (protein making); **smooth ER** makes lipids and helps detoxify poisons and drugs (important in liver cells). ER helps make new membrane — **membrane biogenesis**.
- **Golgi apparatus**: stores, modifies and packages products into vesicles; helps form lysosomes. (Discovered by Camillo Golgi.)
- **Lysosomes**: sacs of digestive enzymes that destroy worn-out parts and foreign material. If the cell is damaged they can burst and digest the cell — '**suicide bags**'.
- **Mitochondria**: '**powerhouses**' — release energy from food as **ATP**. They have their own DNA and ribosomes.
- **Plastids** (plants only): **chloroplasts** (chlorophyll, photosynthesis) and leucoplasts (store starch, oils, proteins). Also have their own DNA and ribosomes.
- **Vacuoles**: storage sacs; in plant cells one large central vacuole provides **turgidity**; in Amoeba food vacuoles digest food.

steps.title: Plant cell vs animal cell
steps.body:
- **Cell wall**: present in plants, absent in animals.
- **Plastids**: present in plants, absent in animals.
- **Vacuole**: large central in plants; small or absent in animals.
- **Centrosome** (helps in animal cell division): present in animals, absent in most plant cells.
- Shape: plant cells are often regular (rectangular); animal cells irregular/rounded.

steps.title: Cell division
steps.body:
- **Mitosis**: one cell → two identical daughter cells with the same chromosome number. Used for **growth and repair**.
- **Meiosis**: in reproductive organs; produces gametes with **half** the chromosome number, so that fertilisation restores the full number.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying ribosomes are membrane-bound — they are not.
- Saying only plants have mitochondria or only animals have them. Both plant and animal cells have mitochondria.
- Mixing up Golgi (packaging) and lysosomes (digestion).

lessons.title: Plant tissues

scenes.text: In Mizoram, Lalremsiama measures a bamboo shoot in his family's grove. It grew several centimetres in a day!
His uncle says grass and bamboo grow from the base of their segments — which is why lawns regrow after mowing.
He also notices coconut husk is tough and fibrous, while a leaf stalk bends without breaking.
Different tissues, different jobs. Let's see how plants are built.

steps.title: What is a tissue?
steps.body: A **tissue** is a group of cells similar in structure that work together to perform a function. Plants are mostly stationary and need a lot of supportive (dead) tissue; their growth is limited to certain regions. Animals move about, so most of their tissues are living.

steps.title: Meristematic (dividing) tissue
steps.body:
Cells are active, with dense cytoplasm, thin walls and prominent nuclei, and **lack vacuoles**.
- **Apical meristem**: tips of roots and stems — increases **length**.
- **Lateral meristem (cambium)**: increases **girth** (thickness of trunks).
- **Intercalary meristem**: at the base of leaves or internodes — e.g. grasses and bamboo regrow after cutting.

steps.title: Simple permanent tissues
steps.body:
Cells that stop dividing become permanent tissues (**differentiation**).
- **Parenchyma**: thin-walled living cells with spaces; stores food. Variants: **chlorenchyma** (with chloroplasts — photosynthesis), **aerenchyma** (large air spaces — helps aquatic plants float).
- **Collenchyma**: living, elongated cells thickened at the corners; gives **flexibility** (leaf stalks, stems that bend without breaking).
- **Sclerenchyma**: **dead** cells with walls thickened by **lignin**; makes parts hard and stiff (coconut husk, seed coats, veins of leaves, jute fibres).
- **Epidermis**: outer protective layer, often with waxy **cutin** to reduce water loss; leaves have **stomata** (pores bordered by guard cells) for gas exchange and transpiration.
- **Cork**: older stems' outer protective layer — dead cells with **suberin**, impervious to gases and water (bottle corks).

steps.title: Complex permanent tissues
steps.body:
- **Xylem**: carries **water and minerals** upward. Elements: **tracheids, vessels** (tubular, dead), **xylem parenchyma** (living, stores food) and **xylem fibres** (support).
- **Phloem**: carries **food** (sugars) from leaves to other parts, in both directions. Elements: **sieve tubes** (with perforated walls), **companion cells**, **phloem parenchyma** and **phloem fibres**. Except phloem fibres, phloem cells are living.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying xylem carries food. Xylem = water; phloem = food.
- Saying sclerenchyma is living — it is dead at maturity.
- Confusing collenchyma (flexibility) with sclerenchyma (rigidity).

lessons.title: Animal tissues

story.title: The sprained ankle at football practice

scenes.text: During football practice in Goa, Joel twists his ankle. The physio, Ms. Rao, says it's a ligament sprain.
'Ligaments join bone to bone; tendons join muscle to bone,' she explains, pointing to his Achilles tendon.
His heart is racing, though he never told it to — cardiac muscle works on its own.
Ice, rest and a proper check-up. Joel decides to learn which tissues make up his body.

steps.title: Epithelial tissue (covering)
steps.body:
Cells tightly packed in continuous sheets with little material between them; rest on a basement membrane. Covers the body and lines organs.
- **Squamous**: thin, flat — lining of mouth, blood vessels, alveoli of lungs. **Stratified squamous** (many layers) — skin, to prevent wear and tear.
- **Cuboidal**: kidney tubules, salivary gland ducts.
- **Columnar**: inner lining of intestine (absorption, secretion). **Ciliated columnar** — respiratory tract, moves mucus.
- **Glandular**: folds inward to form glands that secrete substances.

steps.title: Connective tissue (binding, support)
steps.body:
Cells loosely spaced in a **matrix**.
- **Blood**: fluid matrix (plasma) with RBCs, WBCs and platelets — transports gases, food, hormones, waste.
- **Bone**: hard, strong matrix of calcium and phosphorus compounds — framework and support.
- **Cartilage**: flexible — nose tip, ear, ends of bones at joints, rings of trachea.
- **Ligament**: bone to bone — elastic, strong.
- **Tendon**: muscle to bone — strong, limited flexibility.
- **Areolar**: fills spaces between skin and muscles, around blood vessels; supports and repairs.
- **Adipose**: fat storage under skin and around organs; insulation.

steps.title: Muscular tissue (movement)
steps.body:
Long cells called **muscle fibres**, with contractile proteins.
- **Striated (skeletal, voluntary)**: attached to bones; long, cylindrical, unbranched, multinucleate, with light and dark bands. Moves limbs when we choose.
- **Smooth (unstriated, involuntary)**: spindle-shaped, single nucleus — walls of stomach, intestine, blood vessels, iris, bronchi.
- **Cardiac**: only in the heart; cylindrical, **branched**, single nucleus; contracts rhythmically all life, involuntarily.

steps.title: Nervous tissue (communication)
steps.body: Made of **neurons** (nerve cells), specialised to receive stimuli and transmit electrical messages rapidly. A neuron has a **cell body** with nucleus, short branched **dendrites** (receive messages) and a long **axon** (carries messages away). Nerve cells can be up to about a metre long. Many nerve fibres bound by connective tissue form a **nerve**. Brain, spinal cord and nerves are made of nervous tissue.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping ligament and tendon (Ligament: Bone–Bone; Tendon: Muscle–Bone).
- Calling cardiac muscle voluntary.
- Forgetting that blood is a connective tissue.

For sports injuries: this is general education. Persistent pain, swelling, or inability to bear weight needs a doctor or physiotherapist.

lessons.title: Nutrition: photosynthesis and human digestion

scenes.text: In a potato field in Punjab, sunlight falls on green leaves while farmer Gurpreet waters the crop.
The leaves turn light, water and air into sugar, which travels down and is stored in the potato as starch.
Weeks later, that potato becomes a samosa that Gurpreet's daughter Harleen eats after school.
Her body breaks the starch back into glucose. Every bite of food began as sunlight captured by a plant.

steps.title: Photosynthesis
steps.body:
**Autotrophs** (green plants) make their own food:
**6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O** (in presence of sunlight and chlorophyll)

Three events: (1) **absorption of light** by chlorophyll, (2) light energy converted to chemical energy and **water split** into hydrogen and oxygen, (3) **reduction of CO₂** to carbohydrates.

CO₂ enters through **stomata**, which open and close using **guard cells** (also controlling water loss). Desert plants take in CO₂ at night and use it during the day. Glucose is stored as **starch**. Experiments show chlorophyll, light and CO₂ are all needed (iodine test turns starch blue-black).

steps.title: Other modes of nutrition
steps.body:
**Heterotrophs** depend on others:
- **Holozoic**: take in food and digest it inside (humans, Amoeba — engulfs food with pseudopodia into a food vacuole).
- **Saprotrophic**: break down food outside the body, then absorb (fungi like bread mould, mushrooms).
- **Parasitic**: feed on a living host (Cuscuta / amarbel, ticks, tapeworms).

steps.title: Human digestion step by step
steps.body:
- **Mouth**: teeth chew; **saliva** contains **salivary amylase**, which breaks starch into sugar.
- **Oesophagus**: food pushed by **peristalsis** (rhythmic muscle contractions).
- **Stomach**: gastric glands secrete **hydrochloric acid** (acidic medium, kills germs), **pepsin** (digests proteins) and **mucus** (protects the stomach lining). A **sphincter** releases food slowly into the small intestine.
- **Small intestine** (longest part): receives **bile** from the liver (makes food alkaline and **emulsifies fats** into small globules) and **pancreatic juice** (trypsin for proteins, lipase for fats). Intestinal juices complete digestion: proteins → amino acids, carbohydrates → glucose, fats → fatty acids and glycerol. Finger-like **villi** greatly increase surface area for **absorption** into blood.
- **Large intestine**: absorbs **water**; waste leaves through the anus.

Herbivores eating grass have a longer small intestine than carnivores, to digest cellulose.

steps.title: Everyday connections
steps.body:
- **Acidity**: excess stomach acid causes a burning feeling; antacids neutralise it. Frequent pain should be checked by a doctor.
- **Tooth decay**: bacteria act on sugars to produce acids that soften enamel. Brush twice a day and limit sugary snacks.
- A balanced diet with fibre (roughage) helps the intestine move food along.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying bile is an enzyme. Bile has no enzymes; it emulsifies fats.
- Saying digestion of proteins starts in the mouth — it starts in the stomach (pepsin).
- Saying plants release CO₂ only. They respire all the time and also release O₂ during photosynthesis.

lessons.title: Respiration

scenes.text: At his school sports day in Ranchi, Birsa sprints the 100 m and wins. Minutes later his calf muscles cramp.
He breathes hard for a long time after stopping.
That evening, his mother makes bread, and the dough rises with bubbles from yeast.
Both the cramp and the bubbles come from respiration without enough oxygen.

steps.title: Breaking down glucose
steps.body:
Respiration releases energy from food in the cells (not the same as breathing!).
1. **Glycolysis** in the cytoplasm: glucose (6-carbon) → **pyruvate** (3-carbon) + a little energy.
2. Then:
- **Aerobic** (with oxygen, in **mitochondria**): pyruvate → **CO₂ + H₂O + much energy**.
- **Anaerobic in yeast** (fermentation): pyruvate → **ethanol + CO₂ + energy** (used in bread and brewing).
- **In muscles with oxygen shortage**: pyruvate → **lactic acid + energy**; build-up contributes to cramps.

The energy is stored as **ATP**, the cell's energy currency.

steps.title: Human breathing system
steps.body:
Nostrils (fine hairs and mucus filter air) → pharynx → **trachea** (rings of cartilage prevent collapse) → **bronchi** → **bronchioles** → **alveoli** (tiny balloon-like sacs with a huge surface area and a rich supply of capillaries).

**Inhalation**: ribs lift, **diaphragm flattens**, chest cavity enlarges, air rushes in. **Exhalation**: the reverse. Lungs always keep some residual air so gas exchange continues.

**Haemoglobin** in red blood cells carries oxygen; CO₂ is carried mostly dissolved in blood.

steps.title: Respiration in plants and aquatic animals
steps.body:
- Plants exchange gases through **stomata** (leaves), lenticels (stems) and by diffusion in roots. At night they release CO₂; in daytime, photosynthesis uses CO₂ faster than respiration makes it, so net release is O₂.
- Aquatic animals use **gills** to take dissolved oxygen; water has much less oxygen than air, so fish breathe faster than land animals.

steps.title: Protect your lungs
steps.body: Smoking and air pollution damage the alveoli and the cilia that clean airways, raising the risk of lung disease. On high-pollution days, reduce outdoor exertion. Persistent cough, breathlessness or chest pain needs a doctor.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 'respiration' and 'breathing' as the same thing. Breathing is a physical process; respiration is a chemical process in cells.
- Saying plants respire only at night — they respire day and night.

lessons.title: Transportation in humans and plants

scenes.text: At a blood donation camp in Ludhiana, 19-year-old Navneet donates blood for the first time.
The nurse measures her blood pressure: 118/76 mm Hg. 'Normal,' she smiles.
Navneet's younger brother Arjun, 14, asks how blood keeps flowing round and round the body.
On the way home, he wonders how water climbs to the top of a 30 m tree without a heart.

steps.title: The human heart and double circulation
steps.body:
The heart has **four chambers**: two **atria** (upper, receive blood) and two **ventricles** (lower, thick-walled, pump blood). **Valves** stop backflow.

**Path:** body → vena cava → **right atrium** → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → **lungs** (blood picks up O₂) → pulmonary vein → **left atrium** → **left ventricle** → aorta → body.

Blood passes through the heart **twice** per circuit — **double circulation** — keeping oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate. This efficient supply suits birds and mammals, which need lots of energy to keep body temperature constant. Fish have a two-chambered heart (single circulation).

steps.title: Blood vessels and blood
steps.body:
- **Arteries**: carry blood away from the heart under high pressure; thick, elastic walls.
- **Veins**: carry blood to the heart; thinner walls and **valves**.
- **Capillaries**: one cell thick; exchange materials with cells.

Blood = **plasma** + RBCs (haemoglobin carries O₂) + WBCs (fight infection) + **platelets** (clotting to stop bleeding).
**Lymph**: fluid that escapes from capillaries into tissues; carries absorbed fats from the intestine and returns fluid to blood.

**Blood pressure** is measured with a sphygmomanometer; normal is about **120/80 mm Hg** (systolic/diastolic). Persistently high pressure (hypertension) can harm the heart and blood vessels.

steps.title: Transport in plants
steps.body:
- **Xylem** carries water and minerals from roots up. Root cells take in ions, creating a concentration difference so water enters; the main pull, especially in the day, is **transpiration** — water evaporating from leaves through stomata pulls the water column up (**transpiration pull**). Transpiration also cools the plant.
- **Phloem** carries sugars and amino acids from leaves (or storage organs) to wherever needed — **translocation** — in both directions. It uses energy (ATP) to load sucrose and create pressure that pushes material along.

steps.title: Blood donation facts
steps.body: In India, healthy adults (generally 18–65 years, above a minimum weight) can donate blood at licensed centres; staff check eligibility first. One donation can help several patients because blood is separated into components. Donation is safe with sterile, single-use equipment. Blood groups (A, B, AB, O and Rh +/−) must be matched for transfusion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all arteries carry oxygenated blood. The **pulmonary artery** carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs; the **pulmonary vein** carries oxygenated blood.
- Saying phloem moves only downward. It moves both ways.

lessons.title: Excretion

scenes.text: Kavin's grandfather in Madurai goes to the hospital three times a week for dialysis.
His kidneys no longer clean his blood well, so a machine does part of the work.
Kavin, 15, asks the nephrologist, Dr. Selvi, how healthy kidneys manage it.
'Each kidney has about a million tiny filters called nephrons,' she says, and draws one for him.

steps.title: Human excretory system
steps.body:
Two **kidneys** → **ureters** → **urinary bladder** (stores urine) → **urethra**.

Kidneys remove nitrogenous wastes like **urea** (made in the liver), excess salts and water, keeping the body's water and salt balance.

steps.title: The nephron
steps.body:
The **nephron** is the basic filtering unit.
1. **Filtration**: blood enters a knot of capillaries called the **glomerulus** inside a cup-shaped **Bowman's capsule**; water, glucose, salts, amino acids and urea are filtered out.
2. **Selective reabsorption**: as the filtrate passes along the tubule, useful substances (glucose, amino acids, salts and a major amount of water) are reabsorbed into the blood.
3. The remaining fluid becomes **urine**.

Kidneys filter about **180 litres** of filtrate daily, but only about 1–2 litres become urine — most water is reabsorbed. The amount reabsorbed depends on how much excess water the body has.

steps.title: Dialysis and transplants
steps.body: When kidneys fail, toxic wastes build up. **Haemodialysis** (artificial kidney): blood flows through long tubes of semi-permeable membrane in a dialysing fluid; wastes diffuse out. There is **no reabsorption** in the machine. A **kidney transplant** from a compatible donor is another option; in India, organ donation is regulated by law.

steps.title: Excretion in plants
steps.body: Plants get rid of excess water by **transpiration**, release O₂ as a by-product of photosynthesis, and store some wastes in vacuoles, in leaves that fall off, or as **resins and gums** in old xylem. Some wastes are released into the soil.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying urea is made in the kidneys — it is made in the liver; kidneys remove it.
- Saying all of the filtrate becomes urine.
- Drinking enough water and getting regular check-ups (especially with diabetes or high blood pressure) help protect kidneys. This is general education, not medical advice.

lessons.title: Control and coordination: nerves, brain, plant and animal hormones

story.title: The hot pan and the touch-me-not

scenes.text: In Patna, Rupal accidentally touches a hot pan and jerks her hand away before she even feels the pain.
In the garden, her little brother touches a touch-me-not (Mimosa) plant and its leaves fold instantly.
Later, a dog barks suddenly and her heart races — adrenaline at work.
Nerves, hormones and plant chemicals keep every living body coordinated.

steps.title: Neurons and the reflex arc
steps.body:
Information is picked up by **receptors** in sense organs, travels as an **electrical impulse** from dendrite → cell body → axon, and is passed chemically across a tiny gap, the **synapse**, to the next cell.

A **reflex action** is a quick, automatic response. **Reflex arc**: receptor → **sensory neuron** → **spinal cord** (relay neuron) → **motor neuron** → **effector** (muscle or gland). The spinal cord responds before the brain registers pain, saving precious time. The message also reaches the brain.

steps.title: The human brain
steps.body:
The brain and spinal cord form the **central nervous system (CNS)**, protected by the skull, vertebral column and fluid-filled membranes. Nerves from them form the **peripheral nervous system**.
- **Forebrain (cerebrum)**: thinking, memory, learning, voluntary actions; areas for vision, hearing, smell, touch; hunger.
- **Midbrain** and **hindbrain** handle many involuntary actions.
- **Cerebellum** (hindbrain): precision of voluntary movement, **posture and balance** (walking in a straight line, riding a bicycle).
- **Medulla** (hindbrain): **blood pressure, salivation, vomiting** and other involuntary functions.
- **Pons**: involved in regulating breathing.

steps.title: Coordination in plants
steps.body:
Plants have no nerves; they use chemicals and cell changes.
- **Immediate response**: Mimosa leaves fold on touch by cells changing water content (not growth).
- **Tropisms** (growth movements): **phototropism** (shoots towards light), **geotropism** (roots towards gravity), **hydrotropism** (roots towards water), **chemotropism** (pollen tube towards ovule), and tendrils coiling around supports on touch.

**Plant hormones**:
- **Auxin**: made at shoot tips; cells on the shaded side grow longer, bending the shoot towards light.
- **Gibberellins**: stem growth.
- **Cytokinins**: cell division; present in fruits and seeds.
- **Abscisic acid**: inhibits growth, causes wilting of leaves — a 'stress' hormone.

steps.title: Hormones in animals (endocrine system)
steps.body:
**Endocrine glands** release hormones directly into the blood.
- **Pituitary**: growth hormone (deficiency in childhood → dwarfism; excess → gigantism). It also controls other glands.
- **Thyroid**: **thyroxin** regulates metabolism; needs **iodine** — deficiency can cause **goitre** (swollen neck), which is why iodised salt is used.
- **Adrenal**: **adrenaline** — 'fight or flight': faster heartbeat, more blood to muscles, faster breathing.
- **Pancreas**: **insulin** regulates blood sugar; deficiency leads to **diabetes**.
- **Testes**: **testosterone**; **ovaries**: **oestrogen** — changes at puberty.
- Hypothalamus, pineal and others also play roles.

Timing and amount of hormones are controlled by **feedback mechanisms** (e.g. high blood sugar triggers more insulin).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the brain controls the knee-jerk/hot-pan reflex directly. The spinal cord does.
- Saying the cerebellum controls thinking — that is the cerebrum.
- Thinking Mimosa's movement is a tropism. It is a nastic (non-growth) movement.

lessons.title: How organisms reproduce: asexual and plant sexual reproduction

scenes.text: Nisha's grandmother in Nashik gives her a cutting of a money plant. 'Put it in water — it will grow roots,' she says.
Their neighbour grafts a rose branch onto a hardy rootstock to get big flowers sooner.
Meanwhile, forgotten bread in the kitchen grows fuzzy black mould.
In the garden, bees carry pollen from flower to flower. Life has many ways to make more of itself.

steps.title: Why reproduce, and why variation matters
steps.body: Reproduction makes new individuals and keeps a species going. The key step is **copying DNA**. Copying is never perfectly exact, so small **variations** appear. Variation is useful: if the environment changes (temperature, water), some variants may survive better — the basis of evolution.

steps.title: Asexual reproduction (one parent)
steps.body:
- **Fission**: Amoeba splits into two (binary fission); Plasmodium (malaria parasite) divides into many (multiple fission).
- **Fragmentation**: Spirogyra breaks into pieces that grow into new filaments.
- **Regeneration**: Planaria and Hydra regrow from body pieces using specialised cells.
- **Budding**: Hydra and yeast grow a bud that detaches.
- **Vegetative propagation**: new plants from roots, stems or leaves — Bryophyllum leaves, potato 'eyes', sugarcane, roses, bananas, oranges. Artificial methods: **cutting, layering, grafting**; **tissue culture** grows many plants from a few cells. Advantages: faster flowering and fruiting, plants without seeds can be grown, offspring are genetically similar to the parent (keeps desirable traits).
- **Spore formation**: Rhizopus (bread mould) produces spores in sporangia; spores survive harsh conditions.

steps.title: Sexual reproduction in flowering plants
steps.body:
A flower's reproductive parts: **stamen** (male: anther with pollen grains, on a filament) and **pistil/carpel** (female: stigma, style, ovary with ovules).
- **Pollination**: transfer of pollen from anther to stigma — **self-pollination** (same flower/plant) or **cross-pollination** (another plant), by wind, water, insects and other animals.
- **Fertilisation**: a **pollen tube** grows down the style to the ovule; the male germ cell fuses with the female germ cell (egg) to form a **zygote**.
- After fertilisation: the zygote → **embryo**; ovule → **seed**; ovary → **fruit**; petals, sepals, stamens usually wither.
- **Germination**: seed grows into a seedling with suitable water, air and temperature.

steps.title: Why bees matter
steps.body: Many crops (fruits, vegetables, oilseeds) depend on insect pollinators. Excessive pesticide use and loss of flowering plants harm bees. Planting native flowers and using pesticides carefully helps farmers and the environment.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling pollination 'fertilisation'. Pollination moves pollen; fertilisation is fusion of gametes.
- Saying the ovule becomes the fruit — the **ovary** becomes the fruit; the ovule becomes the seed.
- Confusing regeneration (body parts grow into organisms) with healing of a wound.

lessons.title: Human reproduction and reproductive health (factual)

scenes.text: Before the reproduction chapter in a Delhi school, Dr. Fernandes asks Class 10 to write questions anonymously and put them in a box.
The box fills up: 'Are body changes at puberty normal?', 'Why do periods happen?', 'What is a nightfall?', 'How do STIs spread?'
She answers every question calmly and scientifically. Nobody giggles for long — the facts are interesting.
'Your body is normal. Respect yourself and others. And you can always talk to a trusted adult,' she ends.

steps.title: Puberty: the body gets ready
steps.body:
**Puberty** usually starts between about 8–13 years in girls and 9–14 in boys, and timing varies a lot — early or late is often normal.
Common changes in everyone: growth spurt, hair in the armpits and genital area, oilier skin and pimples, stronger body odour, new feelings and emotions.
- In girls: breasts develop, hips widen, **menstruation (periods)** begins.
- In boys: voice deepens, facial hair, the body starts making sperm; **nightfall (wet dreams)** — release of semen during sleep — is a normal, harmless part of growing up.
These changes are triggered by hormones (oestrogen and progesterone from ovaries; testosterone from testes).

steps.title: Male reproductive system
steps.body:
- **Testes** (a pair) make **sperm** and the hormone **testosterone**. They lie in the **scrotum**, outside the abdomen, because sperm formation needs a temperature slightly lower than body temperature.
- **Vas deferens**: tube carrying sperm.
- **Seminal vesicles and prostate gland**: add fluid that nourishes sperm and helps them move; sperm + fluid = **semen**.
- **Urethra**: common passage for urine and semen (never at the same time), through the **penis**.
Sperm are tiny cells with a tail for swimming.

steps.title: Female reproductive system and the menstrual cycle
steps.body:
- **Ovaries** (a pair) contain immature eggs from birth; from puberty, usually **one egg is released each month** (ovulation). They make **oestrogen and progesterone**.
- **Oviduct (fallopian tube)**: carries the egg; **fertilisation** usually happens here.
- **Uterus**: muscular, elastic organ where a baby develops. Opens into the **vagina** through the cervix.

**Menstrual cycle** (often about 28 days, but anywhere from about 21–35 days is common): each month the uterus lining thickens to receive a fertilised egg. If fertilisation does not happen, the lining breaks down and leaves the body as blood and tissue — the **period**, lasting about 2–8 days. Periods are healthy and normal; use pads, cups or tampons and change them regularly for hygiene. Very heavy bleeding, severe pain, or periods stopping for months should be checked by a doctor.

steps.title: Fertilisation and pregnancy
steps.body:
During sexual intercourse, sperm may be deposited in the vagina and travel to the oviduct. If a sperm fuses with an egg, a **zygote** forms. It divides and the embryo **implants** in the uterus lining. The **placenta**, a disc-shaped tissue, connects the embryo to the mother's blood supply: it supplies nutrients and oxygen and removes wastes, without the two bloodstreams mixing directly. Development takes about **nine months**; then the uterus muscles contract rhythmically during childbirth.

Pregnancy can begin at the first intercourse and even without full intercourse if semen is near the vagina.

steps.title: Reproductive health, law and safety
steps.body:
**Contraception** (preventing pregnancy):
- **Barrier** methods: condoms (male/female) — also the main protection against **STIs**.
- **Hormonal** methods: oral pills, which change hormone balance.
- **Intrauterine devices** such as the **copper-T**, fitted by a doctor.
- **Surgical** methods: vasectomy (vas deferens blocked) and tubectomy (oviducts blocked) — usually permanent.

**Sexually transmitted infections (STIs)**: bacterial — gonorrhoea, syphilis; viral — HIV (which can lead to AIDS), warts (HPV). Many can be prevented by condoms and tested for and treated; HIV is also spread by shared needles and infected blood, not by hugging, sharing food or toilets.

**In India**: the age of consent is **18** under the **POCSO Act, 2012** — any sexual activity with a person under 18 is a crime, even with their 'agreement'. Determining the sex of a foetus for sex-selective abortion is **illegal** (PCPNDT Act). Sexting or sharing intimate images of anyone under 18 is a serious offence, even among teens.

If anyone touches you in a way that feels wrong, or pressures you, tell a trusted adult or call **1098** (Childline) or **112**. For feelings, relationships and body-image questions, see the **Mann** (wellbeing) school.

steps.title: Myths vs facts
steps.body:
- *Myth*: nightfall makes you weak. **Fact**: it is normal and harmless.
- *Myth*: girls should not bathe, exercise or go to school during periods. **Fact**: normal activities, bathing and exercise are fine and often help.
- *Myth*: the mother decides the baby's sex. **Fact**: the father's sperm (X or Y) determines it — see the next lesson.
- *Myth*: you can tell someone has an STI by looking at them. **Fact**: many STIs have no visible signs; only tests can tell.

items.q: I am 13 and my periods are irregular. Is something wrong?
items.a: In the first year or two after periods begin, irregular cycles are very common as hormones settle. If periods are extremely heavy, very painful, or stop for 3 months or more, talk to a parent and a doctor.

items.q: I woke up with wet shorts. Did I do something wrong?
items.a: No. That is nightfall (a wet dream) — semen released during sleep. It is normal for boys during puberty and does not harm health. Just wash and change.

items.q: Why do some friends grow earlier than others?
items.a: Puberty timing varies by several years and depends on genes, nutrition and health. Starting earlier or later is usually normal. Very early (before about 8 in girls or 9 in boys) or very late changes are worth checking with a doctor.

items.q: Can HIV spread by sharing a water bottle or hugging?
items.a: No. HIV spreads through certain body fluids — unprotected sex, shared needles, infected blood, and from mother to baby without treatment. Everyday contact does not spread it.

items.q: Someone online is asking me for private photos. What should I do?
items.a: Do not send any. Block and report the account, keep the messages as evidence, and tell a trusted adult. In India you can also call 1098 (Childline) or report at the national cyber-crime portal. It is not your fault.

items.q: Who can I talk to about feelings or relationships?
items.a: A parent, school counsellor, doctor or another trusted adult. The Mann school on VidyaVerse has courses on emotions, consent and healthy relationships. For mental-health support in India, Tele-MANAS is 14416.

lessons.title: Heredity: Mendel's laws and sex determination

story.title: Why does Riya have Grandpa's dimples?

scenes.text: At a family wedding in Kolkata, everyone says 10-year-old Riya has her grandfather's dimples — though neither parent has them.
Her cousin Aditya, studying for Class 10, says: 'Traits can hide for a generation!'
He tells the story of Gregor Mendel, a monk who studied pea plants in a monastery garden in the 1850s–60s.
Mendel's simple ratios — 3 : 1 and 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 — explain how traits pass on.

steps.title: Genes and traits
steps.body:
**Heredity** is the passing of traits from parents to offspring. Traits are controlled by **genes** (segments of DNA on chromosomes). Each individual has **two copies** of each gene — one from each parent. Different forms of a gene are **alleles**.
- **Dominant** allele (capital letter, T) shows its effect even with one copy.
- **Recessive** allele (small letter, t) shows only when both copies are recessive (tt).
- **Genotype**: the gene combination (TT, Tt, tt). **Phenotype**: the visible trait (tall/dwarf).

steps.title: Monohybrid cross
steps.body:
Mendel crossed **pure tall (TT)** with **pure dwarf (tt)** pea plants.
**F₁**: all **Tt** → all **tall** (dwarf trait hidden).
Self-pollinating F₁ (Tt × Tt):
- TT (tall) : Tt (tall) : Tt (tall) : tt (dwarf)
**F₂ phenotype ratio 3 tall : 1 dwarf**; **genotype ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt**.

The reappearance of dwarf plants in F₂ shows that traits are inherited independently as units and the recessive trait was present but not expressed in F₁ — **law of segregation**.

steps.title: Dihybrid cross
steps.body:
Round yellow seeds (RRYY) × wrinkled green (rryy) → F₁ all **round yellow** (RrYy).
F₁ × F₁ gives F₂ phenotypes in ratio **9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green**.
New combinations (round green, wrinkled yellow) appear, showing that seed shape and colour are inherited **independently** — **law of independent assortment**.

steps.title: Sex determination in humans
steps.body:
Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes; one pair are **sex chromosomes**. Females are **XX**; males are **XY**.
- All eggs carry **X**.
- Half the sperm carry **X**, half carry **Y**.
- X sperm + egg → XX (girl); Y sperm + egg → XY (boy).
So **the father's sperm determines the sex of the child**, with about a 50% chance each time. Blaming a mother for the sex of a child has no scientific basis.

In some reptiles, the temperature at which fertilised eggs are kept decides the sex.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing genotype with phenotype.
- Thinking 'dominant' means 'more common' or 'better'. It only means it shows in a heterozygote.
- Acquired traits (a bodybuilder's muscles, a language learnt) are NOT inherited, because they don't change the DNA of germ cells.

lessons.title: Evolution: evidence and new species

scenes.text: Imagine a group of red beetles living in green bushes. Crows easily spot and eat them.
One generation, by a copying variation, a green beetle is born. The crows can't see it against the leaves.
Over generations, green beetles survive and reproduce more. Soon most beetles are green.
This thought experiment (often used in textbooks) shows natural selection. Charles Darwin described the idea in 1859 after travels including the Galápagos Islands.

steps.title: Acquired vs inherited traits
steps.body:
- **Inherited** traits come from genes in germ cells (eye colour, blood group).
- **Acquired** traits develop during life (a scar, a trained skill, loss of weight due to starvation) and are **not passed on**, because they don't change germ-cell DNA.

Evolution acts only on inherited variations.

steps.title: Natural selection and genetic drift
steps.body:
- **Natural selection**: individuals with variations that suit the environment survive and reproduce more, so those variations become common (green beetles).
- **Genetic drift**: in small populations, random events (like an elephant trampling many beetles) change gene frequencies **without** any advantage.

**Speciation**: when populations are separated (by rivers, mountains), they accumulate different variations; over time, they may become unable to interbreed — a new **species**.

steps.title: Evidence for evolution
steps.body:
- **Homologous organs**: same basic structure, different functions — forelimbs of humans, bats, whales and frogs. They suggest a common ancestor.
- **Analogous organs**: different structure, same function — wings of birds and insects.
- **Fossils**: preserved remains or traces of organisms. Deeper layers usually hold older fossils; dating also uses radioactive isotopes. *Archaeopteryx* had features of both reptiles and birds; feathers may first have evolved for warmth before flight.
- **Artificial selection**: from wild cabbage, farmers selected broccoli, cauliflower, kohlrabi, cabbage and kale — showing how selection changes forms over generations.

steps.title: Evolution is not a 'ladder'
steps.body: Evolution produces **diversity**, not 'progress' towards humans. Humans did not evolve from chimpanzees; both share a **common ancestor** from long ago. Modern humans (*Homo sapiens*) originated in **Africa**, and spread across the world over tens of thousands of years. All humans today are one species, and skin colour differences are small genetic variations.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying giraffes got long necks by stretching (that would be an acquired trait — this was Lamarck's idea, not supported).
- Saying 'humans came from monkeys'.
- Mixing homologous (same structure) and analogous (same function) organs.

lessons.title: Our environment: ecosystems, energy flow and the ozone layer

story.title: The fish that made the eagles sick

scenes.text: Farmers spray a pesticide that doesn't break down easily. Rain washes small amounts into a lake.
Plankton absorb a little; small fish eat lots of plankton; big fish eat lots of small fish.
Fish-eating birds at the top of the chain end up with the highest concentration — in the 20th century DDT thinned their eggshells in many countries.
Students in Bengaluru and Berlin both study this story: biological magnification.

steps.title: Ecosystem components
steps.body:
An **ecosystem** = living (biotic) + non-living (abiotic: temperature, rainfall, soil, minerals) components interacting. Natural: forests, ponds, lakes; artificial: gardens, crop fields, aquariums.
- **Producers**: green plants and algae (make food by photosynthesis).
- **Consumers**: herbivores, carnivores, omnivores, parasites.
- **Decomposers**: bacteria and fungi break down dead matter, returning nutrients to the soil.

steps.title: Food chains, webs and the 10% law
steps.body:
A **food chain**: grass → deer → tiger. Each step is a **trophic level**. Food chains interconnect into **food webs**.

Energy flow is **unidirectional** (from the Sun → producers → consumers) and does not return. At each level, much energy is lost as heat and used for life processes; only about **10%** passes on to the next level (**10% law**). So food chains usually have only 3–4 levels. Green plants capture only about 1% of the sunlight falling on leaves.

**Biological magnification**: non-biodegradable chemicals (like some pesticides) accumulate and increase in concentration at higher trophic levels. Humans at the top can be affected.

steps.title: The ozone layer
steps.body:
**Ozone (O₃)** in the upper atmosphere shields Earth from harmful **ultraviolet (UV)** radiation, which can cause skin cancer and damage to eyes and plants. It forms when UV splits O₂ into O atoms, which combine with O₂.

In the 1980s, scientists found ozone thinning, linked mainly to **chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)** from old refrigerants and aerosol sprays. In **1987**, countries agreed under the **Montreal Protocol** to phase out CFCs; the ozone layer is now slowly recovering — a success story of global cooperation.

steps.title: Waste: biodegradable and non-biodegradable
steps.body:
- **Biodegradable**: broken down by microbes — vegetable peels, paper, cotton.
- **Non-biodegradable**: persist for long — most plastics, glass, some chemicals. They can harm animals and soil.

What you can do: **reduce, reuse, recycle**; segregate wet and dry waste at home; compost kitchen waste; carry a cloth bag; avoid single-use plastic.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying energy flows in a cycle. Nutrients cycle; energy flows one way.
- Saying the top consumer gets the most energy. It gets the least energy but often the highest concentration of persistent chemicals.
- Confusing ozone depletion with global warming — they are different problems (though some ozone-depleting gases are also greenhouse gases).
